PROPOSED SUSPENSION OF EXPORT OF NUCLEAR MATERIAL PENDING ADOPTION OF SATISFACTORY SAFEGUARDS-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a motion of urgent and pressing necessity under the provisions of Standing Order 43. My motion is prompted by the rapidly deteriorating ability of the industrialized world to control the proliferation of nuclear weapons. In view of the nightmarish implications of recent reports of the loss of large amounts of uranium, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies):
That the government suspend exports of uranium and nuclear technology until this House is satisfied that the safeguards system is adequate to prevent the threat of nuclear proliferation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to the provisions of Standing Order 43, I ask for the unanimous consent of the House to rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
Considering that the method now used to count the number of unemployed is not fair towards the economically underdeveloped regions, such as the south shore for example, and considering that this tends to reduce certain budgets provided under the Canada Works and Youth Canada Works programs made available to these regions, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier):
That the House instruct the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce to develop a more appropriate method which would tend to establish on a quarterly basis the real number of unemployed throughout Canada.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, one change which certainly must take place is a change in the rates for moving goods from the east to the west as opposed to from the west to the east. speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: ALLEGED RATE DISCRIMINATION AGAINST WEST-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question is not quite as simple as the hon. member seems to indicate. Bill C-33 is a response to a great many of the discussions which followed the economic opportunities conference in Calgary in 1973 and comes after a number of the myths and arguments which had been laid on the table at that time were put to rest. The fact of the matter is that we cannot have every rate exactly reflecting costs without doing a great deal of damage to any possible system of rate setting and removing the usefulness of competition where it indeed can exist. In Bill C-33 we are saying that the railways ought not to have freedom to set rates just on the basis of competition where that competition is inadequate, and therefore some limits on the maximum are required.
The bill in question begins to put those limits in place, and it has a mechanism for progressively lowering that limit to keep the pressure on the railways to obtain their revenues by as direct a relationship as reasonably possible between costs and the rates they charge.

I ask this question because I believe that both at home and abroad there is considerable confusion about Canada's position. There is probably an explanation for it, because we have made a deal with Argentina, which has not signed the international agreements but has entered into a bilateral agreement. We have the Euratom countries; we have the countries which have signed the agreement, and others which have not signed. It is clear that people in Canada and, I suspect people abroad, do not know the Canadian position on the export of nuclear materials and nuclear weapons. I submit that this confusion ought to be cleared up before the minister makes a statement at the important meeting he is to attend.

No matter in the world is more important than this one. Without question, many people think that Canada is a great contributor to this proliferation. I, therefore, hope that before the minister goes to Europe to participate in those meetings which are always kept quiet, he will outline Canada's position specifically.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext: The present system of advance rulings is an administrative procedure which is within the jurisdiction of Revenue Canada and there is no statutory requirement to issue rulings of any sort. In any event, the question of capital versus income gains is one of the most difficult to rule on. It often involves assessing a taxpayer's interest and motivation behind a particular transaction, in relation to his history of conducting his affairs both past and present which is difficult to determine except after the fact. Finance has not considered amending the Income Tax Act to require National Revenue by law to issue such rulings. Strict rules are difficult to set out in law where the particular facts of a single transaction must be assessed against the background of the taxpayer's past history of similar transactions and his motivation for the proposed sale.

speechtext: The House resumed consideration, from Friday, April 29 of the motion of Mr. Marchand (for the Minister of Finance) that Bill C-48, to amend the Farm Improvement Loans Act, the Small Businesses Loans Act and the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE LOANS TO 175,000 FOR IMPROVEMENT OF FARMS, BUSINESSES OR FISHERIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I enter this debate to reiterate and reinforce some of the points made by my colleagues who spoke so eloquently outlining their support for the bill, as well as some areas of major concern with regard to farm improvements and small business loans. I wish to make particular reference to the speech by our lead-off spokesman, the hon. member for High Park-Humber Valley (Mr. Jelinek), and the excellent speeches made by the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Korchinski), the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Smith) and the hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte (Mr. McCain). I support this legislation, which goes back to 1961. It was brought in at that time by a former prime minister of this country, the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker). It has borne the test of time very satisfactorily.
On this occasion we find ourselves in a position where it is necessary to extend the bill for another three-year period. We had hoped that government would have provided the opportunity for advancing some very much needed reform in the area of Financing and capital availability for farm improvements, small business and fisheries. There is nothing new in this bill, nothing to reaffirm the reality of the small business sector and the uniqueness of the difficulties of farmers and fishermen. It is simply a continuation of legislation that has been in effect since 1961. It is an extension. Maximum loan limits are increased, and small business is redefined. However, the provisions of this bill do not meet the realities of the day in terms of the improvement of small businesses, farms and the fisheries.
A very good case can be made for the fact tl at the maximum loan provided under the provisions of this bill is too restrictive and too limited. A case could be made for the fact that the maximum amount to be advanced under the provisions of this legislation should be doubled. My major complaint however, is in the application of loans under the provisions of this legislation-the actual utilization and
Improvement Loans
administration of this bill. In many respects it is unworkable and useless. It has not been proven satisfactory in recent times. The Farm Improvement Loans Act has not worked effectively, and the same can be said for the Small Businesses Loans Act.
Other speakers have pointed out and provided examples of banks refusing to provide funds under the provisions of this act. When a client comes in to make a loan, it is dependent upon the interest rate at that particular time. If the farm improvement loans program is less than the going rate, the client is shifted to a different kind of loan, either a demand loan or a personal loan. In most cases these loans carry a higher rate of interest.
When this legislation was brought forward it was with the acknowledgment that there was something different about the need for financing small businesses and farm improvements. However, the application of this legislation as it presently exists is of no benefit to the majority of those who use it. Cases of refusal under the provisions of the Farm Improvement Loans Act are numerous. On many occasions farmers have complained to me that they had been turned down for a farm improvements loan. I have written to successive ministers of finance, who have acknowledged receipt of my letters, said the situation was wrong and never did anything about it.
This bill would have been an excellent opportunity for this issue to be clarified. If the banks are given a guarantee under the provisions of this act, there should be some obligation on their part. They should be compelled to honour the provisions of this legislation and uphold their obligations. However, that has not been the case. In that sense, I do not particularly like this legislation because it fails to improve that particular aspect of the program.
We all know the banks are not interested in lending money at an unadvantageous interest rate, so they generally shift such loans into a different package. We should know, too, that everything a farmer does today is not profitable. We note from the Canadian farm input index that the cost of commodities which a farmer must buy has risen by 30 per cent since 1973. It is much higher in western Canada. We also note that realized net income for the farm sector in this country was down by some 21 per cent in 1976 as compared with 1975. Moreover, projections for 1977 indicate that realized net income will decline by 46 per cent, almost one-half of the figure in 1975. Looking at the figures in another way, we find the projected level represents only a very modest increase of 11 per cent over the disastrous year 1971.
I want to reiterate the words of the hon. member for Mackenzie who pointed out that there are very serious problems in agriculture at the present time. The government has done nothing to moderate farm input costs. Quite the contrary: it has contributed to them by its recent action in restricting imports of pesticides and chemicals from the United States. This will have the effect of increasing the cost of those items by some 50 per cent.
80012-491/2

May 2, 1977
Improvement Loans
We hear a lot of talk about a national food policy, but we are concerned by the fact that it is being promoted, largely, by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Abbott) whose major interest is to reduce food prices in this country. Mr. Speaker, we are all consumers of food products and are concerned about price, but we must bear in mind the importance of ensuring a stable agriculture industry. It is a major national resource. It needs to be stimulated and strengthened, but that is something the government has failed to do.
We also hear a lot of talk these days about feeding a hungry world and the implications of such a challenge for the food producers in Canada. But if we continue to allow the agricultural industry to drift as it has in the past 14 years of Liberal rule, I wonder whether we shall be able to feed ourselves properly. Canada is now the fourth largest importer of beef in the world. On a per capita basis, we rank close to number one.
In 1975 we were net importers of dairy products and net importers of eggs. We are presently spending one-third of our total food dollar on imports. That figure is based on 1975 statistics. In 1974 we were spending 25 per cent of our food dollar on imported food, and in 1973 the figure was 18 per cent. What a dangerous trend, Mr. Speaker. It is shameful for a country such as Canada, with its capacity to produce and its expertise in this field. The government has failed to provide conditions in which the agriculture industry can thrive. We know that the fruit and vegetable side of the industry is in serious decline.
I am pleased to see in the House the minister in charge of the Wheat Board. Given the fact that the Canadian farm input index shows an increase of some 30 per cent since 1973, it seems appropriate to review the operation of the two-price system for domestic wheat in line with the increase in the cost of commodities necessary for production. I believe there was a commitment on the part of the minister at the time the two-price system was introduced to effect an upward adjustment in the minimum provided under the system so as to reflect increases in the cost of production. I know the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, in its annual submission to the cabinet, has so recommended. The federation is recommending an increase of 75 cents a bushel, which would bring the price to the level of $4 a bushel as a minimum. Bearing in mind the price squeeze in which producers are finding themselves, and the weakening of the international wheat market, I hope the minister will consider an adjustment which would enable the producers to partially recover at least some of the increased costs associated with the production of wheat.
In my view, the agricultural industry is in a dangerous slide, and the lack of serious attention to agriculture in the bill before us is one further example of the government's intransigent attitude toward the farmers of the nation. We hear a lot of talk, and there are lots of gestures, but it is only when the government finds it politically expedient to take action that anything is done. I have in mind the announcement of the dairy policy the other day. In my view, it was totally related to the by-elections in Quebec.

I am glad to see the Minister of State for Small Business (Mr. Marchand) in his place at this time. I know he has been doing a lot of travelling across the country, trying to sound out the views of small business organizations and the chambers of commerce.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE LOANS TO 175,000 FOR IMPROVEMENT OF FARMS, BUSINESSES OR FISHERIES
speechtext: And of the Liberal organizations.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE LOANS TO 175,000 FOR IMPROVEMENT OF FARMS, BUSINESSES OR FISHERIES
speechtext: I am sure he is doing a lot of speaking to Liberal businessmen as well. I do not blame him for that.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE LOANS TO 175,000 FOR IMPROVEMENT OF FARMS, BUSINESSES OR FISHERIES
speechtext: I didn't know there were any.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE LOANS TO 175,000 FOR IMPROVEMENT OF FARMS, BUSINESSES OR FISHERIES
speechtext:
I hope it is not all a political gesture. I say this in all sincerity. The minister's campaign is raising a certain amount of hope and expectation in the small business community, but his success will only be positive if his words can be translated into action in terms of legislation and a realistic small business policy. I hope the hon. gentleman will be successful, and I can assure him and his cabinet colleagues that they will have the support of members on this side for anything which can be done in a positive way to revitalize the small business sector.
It seems to me the first step the minister has to take is to unravel the web of government which presently surrounds small business. This has stymied and choked operations in the small business sector for many years. He can start by simplifying the ground rules. I think he knows that owner-managers cannot occupy their time filling out forms, compiling statistics, worrying about new unemployment insurance regulations, workmen's compensation forms, the application of income tax law, etc. Consider the hardship which will be caused by the introduction of the metric system alone. I wonder how much consultation has taken place with the small business community with regard to that matter. It will cause a great deal of extra cost, frustration and hardship to the small business segment of Canada.
We need regulations and laws which do not frustrate the small business community. We need simple rules, regulations and laws which do not require a small businessman to obtain a lawyer, accountant or a business consultant to explain them. It seems to me there is still a mood prevailing outside wherein the small business community is considered to be a group of sensible, honest people who do not need to be governed by regulation at every turn.
Another problem the small business community has had is the uncertainty of knowing when regulations come into effect and how long they will be in effect. There has been too much uncertainty, and this had created instability. Regulations change at the whim of the government. There are many challenges facing this country, particularly in the small business sector. We have to improve our productivity and our competitiveness. There is a major problem of unemployment. Many of these difficulties can be resolved, perhaps not entirely but to a great extent, by the small business sector.
May 2, 1977

We hear a good deal these days about privatization. I am not sure what it means in terms of the government's proposals. We have heard the word, but have not really had it defined to any great extent. We also hear a lot about "the middle of the road philosophy". A year or so ago that middle of the road philosophy was dead. The free market system was dead. We were going to be subjected to more government intervention and involvement, which created a form of uncertainty and instability. Thus, an unhealthy climate was created for the small business sector. We also heard a great deal about enterprise and self-reliance. There is nothing in this bill, Mr. Speaker, which will serve to endorse those concepts.
I should like to refer to the brief submitted to the government by the Canadian Federation of Independent Business long before this piece of legislation was brought forth. In their February edition of "Mandate", this is what they said:
Research studies by the federation have indicated that about a third of the small business community has suffered slow growth and/or reduced profitability as the result of a lack of owner's equity capital. This lack of capital impairs the ability of a business to secure necessary operating funds and term loans from chartered banks.
There is nothing complicated about that; it is very simple and straightforward. It presents the government with a challenge. The fact that this legislation had to be renewed gave the government an opportunity to consider this very valid and worth-while recommendation. I continue to quote:
The federation, in its brief, made the point that neither the venture capital industry nor government lending agencies can meet the capital needs of small business. Venture capital firms are interested only in high growth companies, usually well off the ground, with the prospect of having their shares sold to the general public ...
In its submission, the federation recommended a series of changes in federal and provincial tax legislation and in the Small Businesses Loans Act-changes designed to free equity and debt capital to finance both new ventures and the expansion of small and medium-size independent businesses.
The use of tax incentives to provide risk capital in small communities would unleash natural financial sources independent of bureaucracy...
The federation also recommended the creation of a new corporation to be called a risk investment company.
In this case investors would receive a tax deferral when the company made equity investments under the same standards as above. Income received by the RIC would not be taxable and shareholders would again be taxed at capital gains rates if their investments in RIC were not realized until after three years...
In the federation's brief, major changes in the Small Businesses Loans Act were recommended:
1.	The limit on loans under the act should be increased from $50,000 to $ 100,000 or even $ 150,000.
2.	Loans should be available for any business purpose, including the financing of current assets.
3.	The interest rate charged should provide enough of a return to the banks that they will actively promote the program.
The capital markets in every country are biased in favour of large established enterprises. Making debt and equity capital available in small quantities is a challenge Canada must face if it is going to create the kind of viable owner-managed enterprises Canada will need in the future.
Those are some very positive, logical and sensible recommendations. Why were they not considered and incorporated in this bill? They presented the government with a golden opportunity. To that extent I regret the fact that very little has been done by the government since the appointment of a
Improvement Loans
minister in charge of small business to deal with the problems facing this sector. There is much that can be done. These recommendations have been advanced by a very effective association, the Canadian Federation of Independent Business. More and more we in this country are realizing that this federation expresses the views and concerns of the small business, owner-managed enterprise.
Small business is not asking for handouts. What is required is essentially an improved climate, recognition of the small business sector as such, that it is something unique and different from the total business sector as it so often is referred to. There must be a major shift in government philosophy. The private sector can carry out much of what government is doing and can do it much more effectively and efficiently. Small business can be more productive and competitive than larger enterprises and can be more labour-intensive. Job-creation in the small business sector is not as costly. I believe it is fair to say that there is less labour-management tension in the small business sector than in the big business sector. Government must assist in promoting new technology and innovations which are developed by small entrepreneurs. There are not many entrepreneurs and innovators in this country, but there is the lack of a climate which is conducive to developing and expanding the creation of innovation and invention which Canadians can provide.
I should like to quote the November 19 submission by the Canadian Federation of Independent Business in connection with this very point. In their brief they say:
Innovation is not dead in Canada as some have suggested, but it is not nearly as prevalent as it could be, and what we have is badly underutilized. Two basic requirements to improve the situation stand out-(1) development funds for individuals and small companies, and (2) marketing of new products, processes and inventions to entrepreneurs and existing industry ...
An interface organization is required to create credibility with the business community, as most large companies are reluctant to deal with inventors.
Government policy, legislation, rules and regulations must be developed in a much more open environment. In this particular connection it seems we have consultation after the fact, not prior or during the consideration of any given piece of legislation. The priority of any government which is concerned with the welfare of small business should be to increase the number and viability of small businesses in this country and their share of the gross national product.
Current programs to encourage small owner-managed businesses are, in my view, completely inadequate. Big labour, big business and big governments have certainly been able to get along quite well in the past, in spite of the numerous economic difficulties.
There is no way we can lump small business in with the big business sector. The small business sector has been subjected to a squeeze, and therefore its growth has been scuppered. This vibrant group needs, and deserves, the help of government. It is a diverse group. Yet there are no comprehensive policies in this country which recognize the diversity and size of this very important group in our economy. We have over 60 per cent of

May 2, 1977
Improvement Loans
the Canadian labour force employed in small business, yet we do not even have a reliable set of statistics in this country upon which we can analyse, in any accurate fashion, the many aspects of the small business community.
There is need for a clear policy for this very large and diverse group of enterprises. We should all recognize and reiterate the importance of the small business sector as probably being one of the most productive, efficient and innovative sectors of our economy. I have a feeling that over the last eight or ten years, under the current administration, the spirit of enterprise and the pride of entrepreneurship have been smothered and the spirit of self-reliance is dead. It is dead because there has been this overly oppressive government dealing in a climate of uncertainty and lack of stability. There has been intrusion and indifference toward small business. One of the problems is that in this country in the last few years we have lumped the small business sector with the big business sector. The two are completely different.
I cannot help but recall the attack on the business community in the campaign of 1972 and, indeed, in 1974 by the former leader of the New Democratic Party. All businesses were lumped together as being "corporate welfare bums." "Profit" was a dirty word. In my view, the former leader of the New Democratic Party did a great disservice to small business in this country, and that is regrettable.
The attack upon the business community by the former leader of the New Democratic Party has created a mood of suspicion and mistrust throughout the whole business world. I am not only referring to large business but, indeed, small business. This innuendo and socialist rhetoric, aided and abetted by the media, has created a disservice to Canada and to the small business community. Many Canadians have suffered as a result of this unwarranted attack, and many businesses have died. The job we have to do now is recreate a climate of confidence, a climate of stability, a climate where initiative and innovation will be rewarded, and a climate of self-reliance.
I believe the minister who has been given the very onerous responsibility of bringing into reality positive measures which will restore significantly the confidence of small business in this country is sincere, and I believe he will attempt to do everything in his power to bring about that favourable climate. His biggest problem will be to gain the support of his other cabinet colleagues who may not be as conducive and as warm to the small business community as I am sure the minister has been as a result of his peregrinations across the country.
I see the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer) in effect saying, "Yes, I am." I commend him for that. He has set an example in expanding the opportunity for small business enterprises to bid on government services and the supply of government materials, for which I commend him. We recognize, in this House, the importance of the small business sector. I want to reiterate that we will support any positive measures to facilitate the growth and the expansion of this very vibrant sector. We will, at the same time, badger the minister. We may not harass him, but we will certainly remind him of his obligations and his responsibilities to this very

important element in our society. We hope that among us we can rekindle the spirit of enterprise in this country. We hope that among us we can serve to overcome some of the major economic difficulties which we face. I want to say to the minister that he should not waste any time in seeking redress to some of the very serious omissions in this piece of legislation.
The principle of the bill is fine. It has withstood the test of time since 1961. It has to be upgraded and advanced in order to recognize the realities of the day. I hope the minister will consider seriously some of the very important recommendations that have been advanced by the Canadian Federation of Independent Business and some of the very important recommendations that have been advanced by colleagues on this side of the House who have taken this bill to be a very serious one and have also taken it as an opportunity to speak about this very important element in our society.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE LOANS TO 175,000 FOR IMPROVEMENT OF FARMS, BUSINESSES OR FISHERIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to speak today in the debate on this measure, for a number of reasons. One main reason is that the matters referred to in the bill have great bearing upon my constituency because small businesses and agriculture constitute a major portion of the economy in my area. Thus, we have the motion moved by the hon. Minister of State for Small Business (Mr. Marchand), for the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald), to amend the Farm Improvement Loans Act, the Small Businesses Loans Act and the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act.
As far as the third aspect of this measure is concerned, there was a time when I had greater interest in, or more active participation in debates on matters as far as fisheries are concerned. In the previous redistribution, the section of my riding that was vitally affected by the fisheries legislation was moved into another one. Although there is a minor part in my riding at the present time, I believe other colleagues of mine will deal more effectively with the particular measure dealing with the fisheries industry.
Compared with former years when we had the opportunity to discuss issues at considerable length in committee of the whole, the opportunity to do so now is very limited. I well remember when measures were brought before the House and debated for considerable time, but recently any debates of considerable length have been looked at with disfavour by the present government and every effort is made to move the legislation forward as rapidly as possible. We agree that it should move as rapidly as possible, but I say that it should be dealt with effectively before further stages of discussion take place.
As we look at this measure dealing with small business, agriculture and fisheries, we find these constitute three very important sectors of our national economy. The bill curtails our ability effectively to deal with the measures, because any one of these three areas should be the topic of real debate and discussion in the House. However, we have to face the facts of life and, as it is now, these matters are being dealt with at the
May 2, 1977

same time. In the first instance I want to deal with the Small Businesses Loans Act. Some time ago I had the opportunity of discussing this legislation at some length. That was in April of 1974 when a similar measure was before the House.
On that occasion I dealt somewhat extensively with the act. Problems still face that sector of our economy. I agree with the former speaker, the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazan-kowski), that while this measure is acceptable, it does not really introduce any new approaches or initiatives to the small business sector of our economy. Small businessmen are still finding extreme difficulty in obtaining adequate capital financing.
I am sure that every member of the House receives a stream of letters and communications from small businessmen who face real difficulties in endeavouring to secure adequate financing which they require to expand their facilities, to update their equipment, and so on. I have many such letters on my files. I find that if a person does not particularly need money, it is available to him; but if he really needs investment capital, it is extremely difficult to find a source from which to obtain this money. I* am speaking not only of the Small Businesses Loans Act but of the other acts under the jurisdiction of the federal government dealing with loans. All applicants are finding extreme difficulty in obtaining funds.
It seems passing strange to me that a government which says it is vitally concerned and interested in this matter, and will set up another organization or expand an agency for this purpose, does not adequately deal with the problem so that in the final analysis those who need capital can obtain it from federal institutions. In the matter of high interest rates, the Minister of State for Small Business alluded to the fact that it is not a problem so far as businessmen are concerned: the problem, rather, is the availability of capital. I suggest that both these matters are of tremendous importance to the businessman, not only the availability of capital but also high interest rates which are required to be paid at the present time. When you consider all the increases in the cost of doing business, and put it against the rate of interest which a businessman has to pay, you find that he is certainly up against a problem that is almost insurmountable.
Then there is the matter of the rate of taxation. I do not know why, but there seem to be ways in which large businesses can obtain tax incentives and an easing of the tax burden. However, small businesses pay the full shot and carry the whole load. This is a burden that is crushing the small business operator, and in many cases makes it impossible for him to carry on his operation.
Another matter that I referred to two years ago when I was speaking on this measure is the massive amounts of paperwork required by governments. I know there is a suggestion that this will be eased for some small businesses. But it seems to me that the paperwork required takes up far more time and attention than an average small businessman is able to give it. It requires the hiring of additional help and adds to his cost of doing business. As far as I can ascertain, a great deal of information that they are required to file is of absolutely no
Improvement Loans
importance to the operation of the national economy, let alone to that of the small businessman. But someone figures that perhaps we should know something about this and that, and perhaps we should create some jobs. So more paperwork is added to the job. I think this is something that the Minister of State for Small Business should take under advisement. We find that additional regulations, restrictions and red-tape contribute to the problem which the businessman has in conducting his business.
I do not think it is necessary for me-although I am ready to do so-to convince the House that we in this party are vitally concerned about the plight of the businessman. I will not put on the record again the recommendations made by the Canadian Federation of Independent Businessmen. My colleague, the hon. member for Vegreville did this excellently. I would like to impress upon the minister and the government the importance of looking very carefully at this particular brief because it is concise, well thought-out and, in a real sense, presents the needs of the small business community. I believe every consideration should be given to their recommendations and statement of policy.
I would like to refer to a statement that was made by my leader when he was speaking in Winnipeg on October 21, 1976, with reference to the small business community. He said:
Other countries, such as Japan, West Germany, and the United States, have governments with a genuine commitment to the small business sector and who support that commitment with concrete and positive policies. Purchasing policies, for example, such as those in the United States by which smaller firms are guaranteed the right to compete for a significant percentage of government contracts and subcontracts. Tax policies that encourage, not discourage, the development of small family or employee-owned businesses and which permit such businesses to be passed along to new generations without prohibitive tax penalties-support programs which help ensure that small business managers have access to top-flight management training programs and, even more important, to venture capital sources in order to expand and develop their enterprises.
That presents in a very concise and clear fashion the views of the leader of this party who is sometimes charged with not making policy statements. I think these outline very clearly his thinking with regard to the small business community. On March 28, 1977, the hon. member for High Park-Humber Valley (Mr. Jelinek) moved the following motion in the House of Commons:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of implementing programs to assist the development of small business in this country, consisting of such positive initiatives as (a) allowing tax credits for investment in small business (b) providing assistance in the formation of small business export consortia (c) changing government tender practices so that small business supplies a portion of government purchased goods and services (d) reducing the government paperwork burden imposed on small business.
I think that, again, sets out our views regarding the importance of this particular sector of the economy. We welcome the introduction of this legislation as far as the small business community is concerned, but I would say it is a very small gesture in face of the real problems confronting the small business community.

May 2, 1977
Improvement Loans
As I indicated in my intervention, I raised these matters in the House some months ago. Again, I compliment the minister for introducing this measure. We urge him to keep working at the job. I believe he has been doing this. We wish him success in his efforts to encourage and assist individual entrepreneurs in their efforts to provide for themselves and their families an adequate standard of living and provide a very important service to the community. I believe that is a very important part of the role of small business, contributing to the local community, perhaps in a more personalized way than larger operations are able to contribute.
I think there is a need for this type of operation. The individual entrepreneur chooses to spurn the "cog and wheel" philosophy which is generally accepted. He chooses, rather, to make his own way, to carve out his own future, and I believe he ought to be encouraged to do so.
The second part of the bill to which I should like to refer is the reference to the agricultural community. This is a very important sector of the Fraser Valley economy. The maintenance of a viable agricultural industry is, and must remain, a priority objective in our national life. While the concept of the family farm is considered by many to be out of date, 1 am firmly convinced that its elimination, either by neglect or design, would not be in the best interests of our nation.
The production of food as the major objective of agricultural activity is not questioned, but there are many other desirable objectives which are achieved by the maintenance of the family farm concept. I point out the fact that in spite of the tremendous obstacles the farmer faces, particularly in getting established in the industry, there are still those who choose to be engaged in the production of food for the nation and for the world. I think there is an individuality which is particularly characteristic of those engaged in this particular operation. It seems to me that we are doing a service to the national life of this country by encouraging those who desire to engage in farming operations to do so.
This is a preferred way of life. But not only that. We face problems which are accentuated by urban growth. We hear them referred to in this House. We listen to questions being posed. We read articles about the fact that in another few years perhaps 90 per cent of the population of Canada will be found within four or five cities, leaving 10 per cent in rural areas. I think that would be a tragic development. Everything possible should be done to encourage those who want to remain within the rural environment to do so.
We face economic problems in urban areas. Officials are experiencing difficulty providing the services which are required. There are social problems which are accentuated and aggravated by the density of population. There is an unemployment problem. In view of all these things, we should do everything we can to encourage those who want to remain in the rural environment and engage in farming operations. The maintenance of a viable agricultural industry is in the interest of the individual, in the interest of the nation and in the interest of the world.
We hear much about shortage of food and starvation in many parts of the world. I believe that the maintenance of our agricultural community is of vital importance to all.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE LOANS TO 175,000 FOR IMPROVEMENT OF FARMS, BUSINESSES OR FISHERIES
speechtext:
I wish I could expand on some of the problems which are being faced, but they are possibly outside the ambit of the legislation now before us. I will have to reserve them for a later time. However, I suggest that in endeavouring to meet the challenge of competition, Canadian producers are facing tremendous difficulties in obtaining the necessary capital to upgrade and expand their operations.
I should like to refer to Canadian Farm Economics of December, 1976. On page 19 of this review there is an article by Dr. R. S. Rust, of the special studies section, farm and rural development division, economics branch, Agriculture Canada. Dr. Rust states the following:
In 1974 and 1975, there were very large increases in the amount of credit extended, caused mainly by attractive grain prices and expectations of continued high rates of inflation. The amount extended in 1976 is believed to have been slightly less than in 1975 because of expectations for lower grain prices, a decrease in supply of credit from some sources, anticipation of lower inflation rates and fewer farms being available for purchase at prices that reflect the changed agricultural outlook.
With regard to the forecast for 1977, I quote Dr. Rust as follows:
The total amount of farm credit extended in 1977 may fall below the 1976 level unless farm income prospects for grains and livestock improve early in the year. Short-term credit is likely to be the only one to show an increase. Interest rates will continue relatively high and though the prime lending rate of chartered banks dropped by one half of one percent in late 1976, further decreases in 1977 will be very slight, if they do occur.
In making these predictions, and in making reference to the past it seems to me that Dr. Rust is pointing out that in 1977 credit will be tighter than it has been in the past and that this will further affect those who require capital for the expansion of their operations and for carrying through their agricultural programs. As I pointed out with reference to the small businessman, the farming population is finding it extremely difficult to have their needs met either through government or private sources of capital.
The extreme difficulty faced by young people endeavouring to establish themselves in agriculture is also a major problem. So as one examines the provisions of this bill, one finds that it does not seem to include any changes which take into account the difficulties of those engaged in agriculture. The bill does not seem to envisage the taking of new initiatives. No new initiatives are taken in the bill which will expand the availability of assistance to the agricultural community. Therefore, all we are considering, really, is another statement in the form of this bill saying that this program is to be continued.
One could say that loan limits are to be increased. I say that the amount provided by the bill is far less than that which is required in order to enable our agricultural community to meet its problems and finance its operations. As it is, farmers face great difficulty in making ends meet. However, we wel-

May 2, 1977

come this legislation in so far as it affects the agricultural community, but urge the government to look at new initiatives and new programs which will meet adequately the needs of those engaged in the agricultural sector of our economy.
I said at the beginning of my remarks that I did not intend to deal at length with the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act. One finds in the field of fisheries, that tremendous changes are taking place. New regulations put forward by the federal government are having a drastic effect on the fishing industry. The independent fisherman is finding it very difficult to finance the equipment and facilities required in order to maintain the viability of this most important sector of our economy.
I appreciate this opportunity to make a few comments, Mr. Speaker. They are not as full or as complete as I would wish. I will have more to say on the subject on another occasion when we shall have the opportunity to deal with some of the other problems facing our people engaged in the three areas of endeavour coming under the aegis of this bill.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE LOANS TO 175,000 FOR IMPROVEMENT OF FARMS, BUSINESSES OR FISHERIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the House is considering second reading of Bill C-48 which seeks to amend the Farm Improvement Loans Act, the Small Businesses Loans Act and the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act. Naturally, we welcome this amending legislation. Any legislation which provides additional support for our farmers, fishermen and small businessmen is welcome. This bill is particularly welcome in the riding I have the honour to represent.
I submit that this bill does not go far enough to do those things it has been purportedly designed to do. The government says that this bill is an improvement and will increase small business eligibility from $1 million to $1.5 million of gross sales. As well, it will increase the maximum loan limit from $50,000 to $75,000. That is to say, the maximum ceiling on loans made under the three acts the bill seeks to amend is to be raised to $75,000. It is clear to me that this new ceiling simply keeps pace with inflation. The bill should have offered much more, such as higher maximums, higher annual gross revenues for eligibility, an increase in the number of institutions offering these loans-that is, institutions other than chartered banks ought to be included-and a far greater variety of reasons whereby people could qualify for loans. In this regard I am thinking not only of those engaged in small business; I am also thinking of farm improvements. The government cannot continue forever to deal with a complex segment of the economy, our agricultural segment, on an ad hoc basis. An over-all policy must be established for the agricultural community, a policy which should take cognizance of financing difficulties, one of the great difficulties our agricultural community faces.
One big problem with the type of loan this bill envisages is that the banks are the last people who want to lend money at a lower rate of interest. They are not going to look for 9 per cent loans when they have no trouble putting out their money on the market at 13 per cent. That shows why this sort of legislation has not worked. If the provisions of the bill are not changed, people will be able to say, three or more years after it has been passed, "You might as well have not brought it in." It
Improvement Loans
will not make any difference to the farmer three years or even 15 years after it is passed. Actually, the people it was designed to help will not be any better off in three years or 15 years than they were before the bill was passed if changes are not made. Banks at present simply disregard this legislation, or disregard it to a great extent. For that reason, I suggest that we should pass legislation which will force the banks to bring a certain percentage of their farm loans under this act. Such legislation would guarantee that the provisions of this bill would be put to sensible use and for the purposes for which they were designed in the first place.
It has also been suggested that the banks should be obliged to submit to the government reports of all applications made under the Farm Improvement Loans Act, the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act and the Small Businesses Loans Act, giving the reasons why loans are refused. Failure to implement this sort of suggestion will mean that the banks will retain control over the economy of our country as is the case today.
In bringing forward this bill, the government has done nothing for the small businessman, farmer or fisherman. Actually, it could be said that the introduction of this bill will make conditions worse, because its passage will prolong a situation which is already detrimental for those segments of the economy. The acts this bill seeks to amend have not been properly administered. Because they could lend money at rates higher than rates specified in those acts, the banks have not been anxious to lend money under the legislation. The fact that so few businessmen have their needs met by this legislation is proof enough there is something wrong with it. Businesses not covered by this legislation must pay interest at the prime rate, plus an additional rate. Let us begin to think about the small farmer, businessman and fisherman, for their problems are growing every day and this government does not seem ready to do anything meaningful about them.
I suggest that $75,000 these days is not a great deal of money. At least, I suggest that not many farmers, fishermen or small businessmen would consider it a large sum of money. You cannot buy much new equipment with it, build many buildings or buy large boats with $75,000. In these days a big tractor or super-combine costs almost that sum. Therefore, as I suggested, the increased loan ceiling does little more than compensate inflation which has been afflicting the farmer, small businessman and fisherman.
It is contended that the banks have failed to meet the needs of the remote areas of our country and this failure has been instrumental in the rapid increase in the use of credit unions. It is suggested that those institutions should also be able to make loans under this legislation. Many farmers applied for farm improvement loans through the chartered banks and were told that funds were not available. Many times they were told that such and such chartered bank, or such and such branch, had used up the allocated amount. However, they were told that money would be available at regular interest rates 2 per cent or 3 per cent higher. In fact, many times they are 2 per cent or 3 per cent higher than the prime rate.
5190

Improvement Loans
This bill is a step in the right direction. However, I must point out that equipment and building costs within the farm structure have doubled in the four-year period. Labour and fuel costs have more than doubled. In one year the cost of pesticides increased 50 per cent. Therefore, in my opinion anything less than doubling the limit of farm improvement loans is not adequate. I ask the government to take this fact into consideration before this bill becomes law.
The decision as to whether to make a farm improvement loan should not rest entirely with the bank manager. His decision can make or break a small businessman or farmer. There should be an excellent reason for refusing one of these loans. When there is refusal, the Department of Finance should be advised. In that way they would monitor the operation of this act. If a farmer, small businessman or fisherman meets the criteria, the bank should make the loan available. I have raised this matter several times in the House of Commons, as well as privately with different ministers of finance over the years.
On numerous occasions constituents have told me that they think they are eligible for a farm improvement loan but the bank says there is no money available for that purpose. On occasion when they go to another bank they are told that they can have a farm improvement loan provided they transfer all their business to that bank. This indicates that farm improvement loans are available. But the banks do not want to make them because they have a lower interest rate. I suppose this is normal, especially when money is in short supply.
During the past three years, farming has been prosperous. Banks did not require the same guarantees as in previous years. When I say that farming has been good for the past three or four years, I do not include the beef farmer. We must look to the future, because if the act is passed that is when it will take effect. The future looks pretty grim, with swiftly rising costs for everything the farmer needs to produce his product. We all know how costs have gone up over the past several years. Net income will drop. Grain prices are dropping except for soybeans, which go up and down, unless the drought in western Canada and the United States causes grain prices to stay up. If these people have very much reduced crops, or no pasture, their income will be disastrous. If that situation develops and higher prices come about, it will not be anything to crow about because it will be at the expense of someone else. That is not a very satisfactory way of getting higher prices.
I now want to deal with the number of loans that were made. I will begin with my province of Ontario. I have here the annual report. Last year there were 3,551 loans made in the province of Ontario. The different amounts are broken down. For all of Canada there were 30,800 loans made, for a total of $202 million. I want to take hon. members back to 1965, when there were three times as many loans made. In 1965, 91,000 loans were made in Canada. I hope we have not lost that percentage of farmers over 11 years. But this indicates that farm improvement loans are not being made use of in the same way as they were 11 years ago. There were 757
(Mr. McKinley.]
small businesses loans made in the province of Ontario, for a total of $11 million. I put these figures on the record to show that the act has not been made use of in the same way as it was 11 years ago.
Many beef farmers have all the farm improvement loans they can get. This is because of the disastrous prices they have received over the past few years. It is shameful that for so long the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) said to the beef farmers that the only way to restrict imports was to form a marketing board, with quotas. The pressure finally got so great that quotas were put on imports to a certain extent. I sometimes wonder whether the minister was purposely depressing the price of Canadian beef, through imports, so that the price would be much improved by the time the next election rolled around. I certainly hope that was not in the back of his mind.
I did not say, as some newspapers have reported, that I am in favour of beef marketing boards. Marketing boards should not be held over the heads of producers indefinitely. This can do great damage, as we saw happen in the poultry industry, causing losses for years. If beef farmers do not want a board, the minister should forget about it.
As this bill passes through the House, I hope the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) will devise some method whereby the Farm Improvement Loans Act, the Small Businesses Loans Act and the Fisheries Loans Act will be much more workable. Other provisions must be looked at in order that these loans will be of some use, particularly to the agricultural industry which is composed of about 5 per cent of the population of this country. Either directly or indirectly, it supports a much larger percentage of the economy.
Related services such as transportation, processing and manufacturing, depend on agriculture as do all the businesses and the livelihood of those engaged in them. It would seem logical that governments would do all in their power to protect and foster this vital industry. Nevertheless, such protection is sadly lacking. A report on fruits and vegetables which was completed more than two years ago has still not been released. Such time-consuming inaction is just not good enough.
The image of the farmer as a labourer in the field is outdated. Today's farmer is a businessman trying to cope with all the complexities of a business world. Thirty years ago, one Canadian farmer fed 12 people. Today, he feeds 50. The increase has resulted largely through increased mechanism. Farmers must have security of protection in order to invest in machinery. Agriculture deserves tariff protection as much as other industries, such as the shoe industry-which is also in trouble today-and the textile industry, which has been afforded some relief recently by way of quota restrictions. The lack of sound Canadian agriculture trade policy at the recent GATT negotiations was not acceptable to me as a member of parliament.
How can the government justify last year's cutback in dairy milk production with a policy to increase cheese imports from 40 million to 50 million pounds? Think of the amount of
May 2, 1977

Canadian milk which could have been used to make that extra 10 million pounds of cheese. It is the equivalent of 500 million pounds of milk. Tariff rates applicable to most agricultural products are levied on a unit basis, a basis which was negotiated at a time when prices were much lower than they are today. Many of those tariff provisions should now be changed to apply the ad valorem tax, enabling farmers to catch up with the effects of inflation past and anticipated.
The people of my constituency have also made representations. The Huron Cattlemen's Association has requested that all government institutions should use Canadian meat products. It has also asked that there be no more restrictions on the use of medication for livestock, but tougher enforcement of the law in cases of the abuse of medication. The association calls for the licensing of the use of Rumensin in cattle-feeding so that Canadian producers can be more competitive with U.S. producers. In addition, the association urges that the practice of paying a rebate, or kickback, on dressed cattle shipped from the west to Toronto and Montreal be outlawed because it creates unfair competition vis-a-vis live cattle dealers in Ontario and the western provinces.
I hope that before third reading of this bill, provision will be made for the setting of interest rates at a level which will enable small businessmen, farmers and fishermen to use the legislation to borrow the money necessary for improvements in their operations. I suggest the rate should be the prime rate, or better, bearing in mind the fact that there is a government guarantee and the likelihood that the net income of small businessmen and those engaged in agriculture will decrease.
Many small businesses are located in rural areas or in towns which chiefly serve the agricultural community. I used to say in my county that as agriculture goes, so goes the county. I still believe this to be true, though not to such an extent as it was 10 or 12 years ago. Since then, industry has moved into many of the towns I have in mind. Nevertheless, there is still a large degree of dependence upon agriculture, and if the farm community can operate in conditions of reasonable prosperity, the small businessmen will need to borrow money in order to keep pace and supply the necessary services.
We realize it is the banks' money which is being used under this legislation, and we know that the banks ought to have a say in deciding where it should go. But if the government cannot work out a satisfactory agreement and see that it is reflected in the bill before us, it will once again have failed the farmer, the small businessman and the fisherman, people who have too often in the past been at the bottom of the totem pole when it comes to recognition. Let it not happen again. If the legislation is not made to work, the government will be doing these people a disservice by allowing a disastrous situation to continue.
It is, therefore, my belief that whatever minister is piloting this bill through the House-probably the Minister of State for Small Business (Mr. Marchand), although I notice the measure is in the name of the Minister of Finance-he should be prepared, when it goes to committee, to give us an indication of how he intends it to work in practice. I am sure
Improvement Loans
members of the committee will want to know what the government has in mind by way of interest rates. I do not find them mentioned in the bill. How is the bill to be administered by the banks? What provisions are being made to monitor its operations to determine whether it is being used in the way intended when the bill was passed? I hope the minister will take my remarks seriously and be ready to give explanations in this regard.

I am grateful to my colleagues, Mr. Speaker, for they know that my remarks in the past have always been most serious. All together we must strive to improve the economic conditions of the Canadian people as a whole, and also make suggestions to the government for introducing new legislation, amending old laws, for the sake of greater effectiveness so that Canada may compete on international markets in the various areas in which we are interested and which are likely to benefit the general public.
During the Easter adjournment, Mr. Speaker, I was somewhat surprised to read in the papers-and I do not intend to level accusations against anybody, for I am suspicious of what I read in the papers-that the House of Commons had adopted only three legislative measures since last October, and that the House's business had progressed slowly because hon. members sitting on this side of the House have unduly and maliciously delayed the proceedings.
Mr. Speaker, if we want our democracy to survive and to last, we must quit picking on members of this side of the House who are here by the will of the people. If we had knowingly impeded the efficiency of Parliament, I would accept willingly such news but it is not the case. The main reason for the delay in our parliamentary works in my opinion is the absence of a schedule which should be prepared at the beginning of a session and which would determine in advance periods when the government would introduce bills which it considered a priority and then in cooperation with House leaders we could establish the number of days or weeks which could be devoted to works and bills considered as a priority by the government.
I think that with a little good will on every part we could come up with such a schedule and thus increase parliamentary efficiency while allowing members of the opposition to assume their full role which is recognized by the Constitution. We cannot be blamed if Canadians have decided that there would be so many members on the government side and so many in the opposition. It is the way democracy works.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I think this had to be made quite clear to demonstrate that I sincerely wanted to participate in the debate on Bill C-48. I shall be brief and concise.
During my remarks, I wish to inform the House that I intend to divide this bill into three specific sectors, which interest more particularly the south shore area, the underdeveloped regions and those which did not get enough assistance from the government. The first part of the bill deals more particularly with agriculture. The government raises the ceiling on loans it guarantees for farmers so they will develop and organize themselves in a better way.
Mr. Speaker, we all recall the 1976-77 dairy year was particularly hard for producers. We remember that the government's dairy policy was extremely disastrous, particularly for the dairy enterprises which planned to extend their business to increase production. And during the spring of 1976-77 many farmers and milk farm owners did buy production quotas. And during the months after the announcement of the dairy policy on April 1, 1976, many of those producers have been denied some of the production quotas they had bought, without getting any reimbursement of the expenses they had made to buy those quotas.
I would call it stealing, Mr. Speaker. It is as if a farmer had bought a cow from another farmer, and then after the cow had given birth since it was productive, the seller went and took it from the purchaser's stable without any reimbursement. That is tantamount to preventing one who has paid for it from taking advantage of something he has bought and which he cannot use. This has done much harm in my area. I am talking about that because it is my duty to do so. I would not like those things to happen again, for it puts producers in difficult financial situations. To survive, they are forced to apply to finance companies for a loan for the next months with the hope that the years ahead will be better.
Mr. Speaker, I just have in mind the case of some producers who came to me this weekend to submit their problems; as a matter of fact they need a loan. But to be able to get from the lender the money they need to keep their business afloat, they are asked to buy new milk quotas. I confess quite frankly that these producers are put in difficult situations. Mr. Speaker, I agree that the government should increase the loan guarantee by several thousands of dollars by amending the legislation. But I do not think this solution will really permit the survival of many farming operations because interest rates are too high. At the same time, the government should legislate to grant loans to businesses. If they are supported, it is because they are weak.
If the government has to help them, this is because they have neither enough vigour nor enough revenues to be able to meet their own needs with their own resources. So I think interest charges should be reduced so that we can really reach the goal of Bill C-48. I do not think it would be reasonable that farm businesses be obliged to pay 11, 12 and 13 per cent interest charges on loans for the development, organization
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Turner).]
and improvement of their farms, without at the same time assuring them that in the years to come they will get stable minimum income and that they will not, as was the case in the past, depend on those having the power to control national and international trade.
Mr. Speaker, a second point I should like to mention before we call it five o'clock, is that it is time we help small businesses. God knows how badly those small businesses in my constituency need some help. There are a lot in the south shore area, in the eastern region, which now face difficult situations. Those people have lots of talent and are capable of managing a business venture, but they are absolutely incapable of competing with the industries in major centres.
Mr. Speaker, I have pointed out repeatedly to the House that industry must be decentralized for the good of the future of our country. Ail our Canadian politicians keep talking about decentralizing it. But those who are responsible for preparing our legislation do not feel deeply enough about it to really act upon it. In passing, Mr. Speaker, I should like to give an example that is characteristic of our times.
Last Wednesday, I had to leave the House to attend a meeting in the town of Montmagny which Belanger-Tappan is in the process of leaving to go to Montreal or its suburbs, namely Saint-Bruno. I would like to mention something appalling: last year, some time during the summer, the workers in that industry, which has been in Montmagny for many years, went on strike, and with good reason, to get salary increases at a time when the average salary was $3.22 an hour; this to my mind is not too much. At the same time, the civil servants of the Societe generate de financement of the province of Quebec sold to Belanger-Tappan the SOMA plants, located in Saint-Bruno, for assembling refrigerators. That is why I say everyone pays lip service to decentralization but no one really does anything about it.
And now, 122 workers may lose their jobs if the company decides to produce refrigerators in the suburbs of Montreal, at Saint-Bruno. The reasons given for moving to the Montreal area are as follows: the cost of transportation is too high, it increases the cost of production and the company cannot compete with its rivals in the same line of production.
That is why I am saying that this government should seriously take into consideration the situation of these small businesses, by giving them some tax deductions and compensations for the cost of transport, in order to reduce the production cost, which would allow them to survive and ensure full employment for the skilled workers who live in that area and are able to work for their country.
Mr. Speaker, I have also in mind the names of a number of small businesses which can just manage to keep going. Yesterday I met representatives from a 20-year old furniture firm. They make low priced furniture which meet the requirements of Canadian citizens. This firm employs more than 140 workers and the personnel manager was telling me only yesterday that, if Parliament does not come up with some legislation or some kinds of measures, this firm will have to close because of the competition from American furniture.
May 2, 1977

Mr. Speaker, it is not without reason that I think the government should bring in amendments to the Small Businesses Loans Act. Here again, I would like those loans to be made at interest rates lower than what is being charged today if indeed we are to achieve the stated objective. Third, this bill applies to fishing industries. I am less knowledgeable about that area but 1 remain convinced on the basis of what I was able to observe listening to the discussions of those who are interested in that field that the same phenomenon applies to the fisheries industry.
I would like, Mr. Speaker, to draw the attention of the House on this important factor in our Canadian economy, particularly at a time when we are going through hours of anguish as there is talk in Quebec of the possibility of a referendum to consult the people to know whether Quebec should separate from the rest of the country. I think we have a very great responsibility in that respect and that we must do everything to try and help those who are in a position to prove that Confederation is viable, that there are equal benefits in all provinces through federal government legislation.
Mr. Speaker, I would also like to draw the attention of the cabinet to a very particular problem which interests us and which is serious. No later than yesterday I met the local authorities of the municipality of Ile-aux-Grues. Of course, Mr. Speaker, that locality is known as the paradise of white geese. It is so true that yesterday on the beaches of Ile-aux-Grues we could admire those millions of white geese that are the pride of this country. Unfortunately, when the hunting season comes we do not have the necessary means of communication to allow those who practice that sport to cross the St. Lawrence to go there.
That leads me to say to you, Mr. Speaker, as well as to cabinet members that there is a very serious communication problem there that must absolutely be solved this year. I am talking about the Ile-aux-Grues and Montmagny wharves. Whether one locates it at Montmagny or Anse-a-Gilles does not matter. What is important is to have good communications to further develop the fishing and hunting industry that is vital to our area. I will certainly vote for Bill C-48 so the situation can be improved. But I would like amendments to be brought in before third reading-
