The House resumed, from Monday, November 15, 1976, consideration of the motion of Mr. Friesen:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider holding a national referendum for the purpose of making a survey of public opinion on the issue of capital punishment at the time of the next federal election.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED HOLDING OF NATIONAL REFERENDUM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I speak on behalf of at least 80 per cent of the Canadian population on this motion calling for a national referendum which has been presented by the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Friesen). Personally, I do not feel that a referendum is necessary, because when 80 per cent to 90 per cent of the people express an opinion on a matter such as capital punishment, we as servants of the electorate should implement their wishes. So I feel that a referendum is a step in the right direction, something that will be welcomed by the 80 per cent or 90 per cent of Canadians who want the return of capital punishment. I believe that the motion is an excellent one and one we should certainly support; that is, that a referendum be held possibly at the next federal election. This

May 2, 1977
Public Opinion on Capital Punishment motion was presented on November 15, 1976, by the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock, who stated:
Mr. Speaker, I have submitted this motion to the House because I believe that many Canadians feel they were betrayed by parliament last summer.
I certainly support those words. That is the exact feeling of the majority of Canadians, that their MPs have betrayed them. The hon. member went on to say:
Never before has there been such a consistently uniform expression to all members of parliament by their electorate as on the issue of capital punishment. For about the past five years every reliable indicator has shown that about 80 per cent of the Canadian people wanted to see a return of the death penalty. Members of the House were fully aware of this desire, yet chose not to ignore it but to recognize it and then to override it. This is why people all across Canada today feel that their elected representatives have betrayed them.
1 can say that I did not betray my constituents, because I voted for the return of capital punishment. The hon. member went on to say:
The Liberal government achieved the majority vote it sought on that issue by using the age-old tactic of the decoy and thereby fragment the opposition. The Liberal cabinet voted as a block and were, in fact, expected to show solidarity behind a government-sponsored bill; but each other member of the House, on the surface at least, was supposed to vote independently. This gave the government not only the advantage of an immediate block of about 28 votes but also the influence of that block for persuading others.
The decoy strategy centred on promoting the idea of a "free" vote or "conscience" vote, incidentally thereby absurdly implying that none of the other votes taken in parliament are either "free" or "conscience" votes. In my mind, Mr. Speaker, that is what has destroyed the respect Canadians ought to have for the institution and the elected members who make up this body. It is this superseding of private wishes over the wishes of the Canadian people that is making every thinking and feeling elector distrust all those men and women who run for public office.
Probably members of parliament have never received more mail than they have on capital punishment. I would like to read a typical constituents' letter into the record. He wrote:
I would like to express my disgust at the government's bill before the House to abolish capital punishment. It is unfortunate that only at election time are MPs interested in what the majority of Canadians want. And the majority want capital punishment to remain and to be enforced.
I believe that in time we will follow the lead of the U.S.A. (as we always do) and return capital punishment. This has been done in many states already. Obviously, they have tried abolition and it has not worked. Why cannot we learn by the mistakes of others?
I hope all Canadians who support retention of capital punishment remember who voted for abolition when the 1978 election comes.
I believe that the members of parliament owe it to the citizens of Canada to call a referendum on this matter. To do otherwise is to misuse the power given to you as an MP.
That is a typical letter of which, I am sure, every member in the House has received hundreds or thousands. There was certainly excellent press coverage on this subject. One editorial appeared in the February 5, 1976, issue of the Walkerton Herald- Times. The headline reads, "Crimes in general would appreciably decline with capital punishment's return". That is the feeling of the majority of Canadians. The editorial reads in part:
We furthermore feel that the gas chamber should take the place of the trap-door when it comes to execution.
A number of suggestions have been made in the House over the last couple of years concerning other forms of capital punishment. I and others have suggested that the subject
[Mr. McKenzie.)
matter be referred to a standing committee where we could discuss alternate methods of capital punishment, but this also was turned down by the government. The article I referred to continues:
Certainly the last hope for Canadians is then that the death penalty at least remain on the books-
But it has been completely removed, even for treason, and the reduction of sentences is unbelievable. The editorial continues:
-even though the government has greatly watered down its deterrent effect by commuting all sentences to life imprisonment.
Most assuredly, abolitionists in general are rendering a truly great disservice to their country and their fellow men, and heaven forbid that they are successful in their ends.
To make matters even worse, there are those completely gutless and totally illogical heads of government who would now even abolish the term altogether.
Also, there were interviews with murderers who opposed abolition. In an article on an interview held in the Drumheller penitentiary, the following was said:
A 25-year minimum sentence for capital murder would turn a convicted killer "into an animal", who would have lost all hope for rehabilitation and might kill again to escape.
That was the message 15 convicted murderers imprisoned in the Drumheller penitentiary gave Sunday to Marcel Prud'homme, the Montreal member of parliament and co-author of a proposed amendment to the capital punishment bill now before the House of Commons justice committee.
Mr. Prud'homme, who drafted the amendment with fellow Liberal Jim Fleming of Toronto, has proposed a 25-year eligibility date for parole in cases of "First-degree murder".
First-degree murder would include murder of a peace officer, prison guard, and murder during a kidnap, rape, or armed robbery. The amendment made no mention of punishment in other cases of murder.
The hon. member went on to say:
The mood of the country is in favour of hanging.
The murderers certainly felt that way, also. In addition, there was a tragic case in Saskatoon of four children being slain. It is most interesting to read the remarks of the father of one of the children, Mr. B. D. Cranfield. He is the father of 12-year old Dahrylyne. The article in the Winnipeg Free Press said that he-
-reacted bitterly to the news of his daughter's death. He said police told him the man arrested had spent time in jail before.
"The way the system is now, they'll probably let him out again", he said.
Mr. Cranfield said he wanted to offer his "congratulations" to Prime Minister Trudeau, federal Solicitor General Warren Allmand and federal Justice Minister Otto Lang, who, he said, have "championed criminals for so long".
"Go ahead, I want everyone to hear," he said. "Politicians have catered to crime. I don't know why they don't offer their own children".
Mr. Cranfield went on to praise the effort made by police in pursuing the case.
This is one of the most tragic cases in Canada, and further evidence of why capital punishment should be restored. At the time we were discussing Bill C-4, a number of excellent amendments were put forward in the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs. I should like to read some of them into the record. I believe they should be discussed again and entered into a new government bill. They read:
(1)	Restore the death penalty for "high treason".
May 2, 1977

(2)	Make the death penalty an alternative, along with life imprisonment, for "treason".
(3)	Restore the death penalty for "first-degree murder".
(4)	Include in the definition of "first-degree murder" a death caused by anyone who previously had committed murder. (This would have the effect of restoring the death penalty for second or third-time killers).
(5)	Prevent the abuse, by the cabinet, of the "commutation" provisions by restricting the use of the so-called "royal prerogative of mercy" only to those cases where there was a specific recommendation for mercy by the jury, or court or in cases where new evidence or fact, not presented in court, were uncovered after the court imposed the death penalty on a convicted murderer.
(6)	Change the death penalty from execution by hanging, to death by-
-any other means which would be more humane or more acceptable to the general public. There are drugs or gases which could be used which would certainly be more humane than the rope. The abolition of capital punishment was of grave concern to the Canadian Police Association, and at the time we were discussing the abolition bill they presented their feelings to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). The following is what that association requested:
Capital punishment must be extended beyond the present limitations so as to include all crimes in which acts of violence result in the death of any person.
Persons who take the life of another while committing such crimes as child molestation, rape, air piracy, political assassination, treason, and robbery must be charged with capital murder and, if convicted, should face the death penalty.
In cases where persons are found guilty of capital murder, after all levels of judicial appeal have been exhausted, and no recommendation for mercy is forthcoming from the judicial process, the federal cabinet shall be prohibited from interfering with that sentence and subsequent punishment.
In cases where a recommendation for mercy is forthcoming from the judicial process the federal cabinet should be permitted to commute the death sentence. However, the alternative to the death sentence should be limited to natural or true life imprisonment.
The supreme court of the United States has reversed its stand on capital punishment. The following was reported by Associated Press:
"The Supreme Court is thinking like the American people are thinking," said a state senator from Maine.
And there was little doubt the court ruling upholding the concept of capital punishment for murders brings the court a lot closer to the thinking of most Americans. Polls have consistently shown strong support for death penalty for murderers.
We in Canada certainly did not get close to the thinking of the Canadian people when we abolished the death penalty, against their wishes. The article continues:
Terry Medgebow, whose son, Joel, was murdered in 1973 in Tampa, Florida, had no doubt the court was right as well as in tune with the nation.
It is unfortunate that this parliament could not get in tune with the nation. A retiring member of the National Parole Board, Mary Louise Lynch, who joined the National Parole Board at its birth in 1960, said in November of 1975 that that may not have been the time to abolish the death penalty. She said that in order to abolish hanging the government might have to impose harsher penalties for other prisoners. The hot climate of public opinion seemed to demand that. She also said the following:
What I'm worried about is that in order to get abolition through, they might require mandatory sentences of 20 or even 30 years ... that appalls me.
Public Opinion on Capital Punishment
Most of them go into prison in their early 20s. Fifty looks like the end of the road to them.
I feel that this is an excellent motion, and in all fairness to the Canadian electorate, which is our master, the government should give serious consideration to this motion, pass it today and allow a referendum on capital punishment at the next federal election.

Mr. Speaker, thank you for this opportunity to speak on motion No. 9. I am rather surprised to see this subject coming up again on the agenda of the House of Commons debates, considering that we had an extensive debate just last year on this subject and that we had a vote which I think most people considered decisive after a series of such debates, many of them over many years.
I would like to give credit to the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Friesen) for his tenacity in moving this motion, if not for some other qualities which are usually necessary in terms of a good motion, such as logic and reason.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED HOLDING OF NATIONAL REFERENDUM
speechtext: He is speaking for the Canadian people; you aren't.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED HOLDING OF NATIONAL REFERENDUM
speechtext:
I believe we take the responsibility to speak for the Canadian people we represent each in our own way. I do not think we need any reminder from any of our colleagues opposite. Sometimes it takes a great deal more courage to pass a measure on abolition than it does to pass capital punishment. Obviously, judging by the previous speeches which have been made on this subject, many of the speakers, and particularly speakers from this side of the House, feel that the issue is not one of capital punishment. We have debated that. The issue here is the forum in which it is presented, that of a referendum, and particularly a referendum at the time of an election. There is obviously some confusion about what a referendum is, how much binding power it has over a government, and the difference between a referendum and a plebescite. It is certainly novel to try to include a referendum at the time of an election. I wonder what confusion that would throw into the whole process. And if we allow one, why not many? There are hundreds, if not thousands, of important issues in a country like this at any given time.
However, I think the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock has a number of serious concerns, and nobody can complain about that. I would like to go over a few of them. In his speech the hon. member began by using the word "betrayed". I think that is much too strong and intemperate a charge to be levelled at hon. members of this House. I do not think one can question the motives of the elected representatives of the people to that extent. We may make mistakes and we may have different ways of doing things. But I do not believe a member of this House has ever come to Ottawa deliberately and consciously to betray the people he was elected to represent.
Related to that was the very strong suggestion in the hon. member's speech that there has been a loss of public confidence in the process of government. That suggestion has been made before. It has been made in other countries, and it has

May 2, 1977
Public Opinion on Capital Punishment also been made about other sectors such as business, the professions and many other parts of society. I think this has some truth, but it is a bit overstated. I think there are other reasons the public tends to react the way it does, with lack of interest, apathy, and so on. We have come through a difficult and rather confusing time. We have come from a period of great growth and expectation to one in which the whole social situation is tightening up and the process of society is becoming very complicated. I believe these problems will work themselves out with time, particularly in a country such as Canada where people are reasonable.
There is also some concern about the role of members of parliament and how they vote. We went through this at great length in the capital punishment debate. Obviously, there is no simple answer and there are differences of opinion. These differences change all the time, but we take notice of what the people think. Surely we have more opportunity to study issues than the people we represent, and when it comes to moral issues quite often it is obvious that members of parliament do make stands. However, we should try to make our views known to our constituents before and between elections. We have been over that many times.
The subject of polls has come up. That is a very hot topic these days. People tend to quote polls when the polls agree with their arguments, and it is interesting and obvious that they do not when the polls go against their arguments. One wonders what we did before polls came along; how we managed to have government and how we managed to represent our people. I think the reasons are obvious. Interesting though they are, we do not place enough confidence in polls to conduct government by poll. We try to test the opinions of our constituents with questionnaires. In my experience no more than 10 per cent of all constituents reply even to questionnaires on the most controversial issues. That, clearly, is not a foolproof method.
The hon. member suggested that the government had resorted to the use of a decoy involving cabinet solidarity and a free vote or conscience vote. I find that particularly hard to understand. If the hon. member had suggested, as did others, that the companion bill, Bill C-83, to do with law and order was the decoy, I could have understood him. He could have argued that it was withdrawn after parliament abolished capital punishment and I would have understood him. But he did not say that. In any event, that argument is not correct, because a general law and order bill which includes gun control is being prepared again for early introduction.
The hon. member also suggested that capital punishment was a non-partisan issue and that every member of the House should have been free to vote as he saw fit, and therefore vote in accordance with the wishes of the people, presumably against abolition. I am not sure the hon. member was being entirely accurate. For example, it is strange that the NDP voted pretty well en bloc against capital punishment, that is, for abolition, whereas the Social Credit Party voted en bloc

against abolition. It is obvious that in my party, in keeping with the definitions of liberalism, respect for individual freedom and minority rights, there was a strong feeling against the retention of capital punishment. Therefore, from the viewpoint of the Liberal party there was, I think I can say until I hear otherwise, a free vote.
The hon. member's argument with regard to elitism, to members of parliament representing themselves and their own point of view, I suggest is not correct. As I said, we should try to put our views honestly to our electors both before and after election. I do not believe, contrary to what the hon. member suggested, that this issue was well publicized and well understood. The question was thoroughly debated in the House and in political circles, but it is a complex subject and I am not under the impression that the average person has studied thoroughly and understands many of the details concerning capital punishment.
It has been suggested that parliament voted against the wishes of the people and that the vote should have reflected the wishes of the people. I think that accusation is cynical. Members of parliament understand the difficulties of the situation, know how difficult it is to arrive at a decision and, as a colleague said, must use their best judgment. By doing this they are working for the people, even though the polls do not reflect this fact. It has also been suggested that in some way redistribution may make this process worse. Frankly, that argument was irrelevant and I did not understand it.
The hon. member mentioned ministers travelling across the country to get consensus. They do this on economic issues. 1 see nothing wrong with it; it is part of our democratic process. But that point, again, concerns a different issue and a different process. It is the sort of thing we all do when we return to our ridings every weekend. Certainly, it should not be suggested that what ministers hear on a trip should influence the legislation they introduce into this House.
One might adopt a position exactly opposite to that of the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock and say that members of parliament must adopt individual positions on moral issues. Sometimes the member of parliament must take a difficult position, one that is different from that of the general public he or she is representing. In this way we can show initiative. Now we are considering a difficult issue, and I find it difficult to understand how we can settle such matters with a vote. Under our system, our people are represented in parliament and they rule through the majority of their elected representatives.
One wonders why we should single out the issue of capital punishment to be decided by referendum, when there are so many other important issues with which we must deal. The question is, why should we hold a referendum at all, especially at election time? The hon. member made some positive points, on which I congratulate him. In making them the hon. member almost answered his own argument. He said previously, as reported on page 1000 of Hansard for November 15, 1976, when debating his private member's motion on capital punishment:
May 2, 1977

Members of the House were fully aware of this desire, yet chose not to ignore it but to recognize it and then to override it.
He was referring to this desire for retention. I think this is quite true, but I suggest members did it sincerely. I suggest that those words apply to members of all parties, including some prominent members of the hon. member's party.

speechtext: No one denies it. Mistakes are made in all parties.

speechtext: Yes, that is true. But those remarks have significance in this debate. The hon. member also said that the Liberal cabinet voted en bloc, that the abolition bill was a government-sponsored bill. Then he said, as reported on page 1001 of Hansard for November 15, 1976, " ... but each other member of the House, on the surface at least, was supposed to vote independently." The hon. member made a positive point. After all, we expect a government to speak with one voice; we do not expect it to adopt a confused or divided position.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED HOLDING OF NATIONAL REFERENDUM

I can only say that I have seen no evidence to show that undue pressure was put on any member of the House to vote one way or another. I remain to be convinced that there was pressure. Third, the hon. member suggested, as reported on page 1001 of Hansard:
-capital punishment as a subject itself was really an exercise of diminishing importance, except for the very important factor of providing the electors with information on how each member established his position and justified his vote.
The hon. member is correct. The subject was debated well, and the public was aware of the debate. At that point, of course, like any other bill, it became a matter of decreasing importance. Other work needed to be done. As well, the hon. member suggested, as reported on page 1001 of Hansard'.
-sometimes this is the case, that it is in fact the job of the member to study issues in detail, to use all the resources at his disposal, resources that may not be available to the general public, and then as a result perhaps arrive at conclusions that are unpopular and possibly misunderstood.
I agree. I do not think anyone could have worded better the role of the temper of parliament. The hon. member has accurately described the role of the member of parliament. I do not necessarily see any exceptions to that role. I do not see why an issue like capital punishment should create an exception to the general rule.
The hon. member also suggested that when the Liberal party was elected in 1974 it took pride in how intelligent and incisive this country's electors were in electing it to govern. I cannot argue with that position, and I doubt if any other member on my side of the House would argue with it either.

speechtext: Don't be too sure.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED HOLDING OF NATIONAL REFERENDUM
speechtext:
By saying that, I am not inviting anybody to suggest that the government and those on the opposite side of the House let the House down. Certainly, this would not have been done intentionally. Actually, by voting as it did, the House showed leadership. Similarly, it is the government's job
Public Opinion on Capital Punishment to make decisions on behalf of the people and so show leadership. I think the hon. member himself suggested this. The hon. member also put forward the position of those who might disagree with him. He said, as reported on page 1001 of Hansard, that they might ask the following questions:
What do you want a member of parliament to be, an automaton, slavishly repeating what he has been told by a partially or ill-informed public? Are we to have parliament made up of a delegate system, where members go home to a committee to receive instructions as to how to vote-
The obvious answer is no, that is not how we want our members of parliament to act, as the hon. member himself suggested. He also said, as reported on the same page of Hansard:
Canadian people don't expect that: they expect members of this House to be capable of intelligent and independent decision-making... they expect honesty at election time.
I certainly agree with the hon. member on both points. He went on to say:
-members of the cabinet have been travelling across Canada trying to get a consensus from various sectors of our economy.
I have dealt with that point, and I think the cabinet is doing what it ought to do. He went on to say, as reported on page 1002 of Hansard'.
I do not think anyone wants to see government by referendum. Members of this House have been elected to be decision-makers.
I am reading selectively to illustrate important points the hon. member made in that speech. The hon. member made exceptions, obviously in favour of the motion we are now discussing. The hon. member must know that many of us do not agree with his motion. Nevertheless, he deserves credit for making a well-balanced case. Many of the things he said are worth repeating.
In a democracy it is easy to be caught up with the notion that the majority is right. It may be, but not necessarily. This, of course, is a plea for flexibility. He goes on to say the majority even has the right to be wrong. That is an interesting and rather strange statement. He says the government should let them do something, even if the majority of the public are wrong.
What about in time of war? If we thought that the public were making the wrong decision, that they were not going to war as they should, or were going to war and they should not, what should the government do? I doubt if we would go along with the public just because they were all on one side of the issue. I again quote:
-the concern of John Stuart Mill, that great Liberal member of the British House of Commons 100 years ago. Always concerned that government should always be sensitive to the rights and feelings of minority groups, he spoke out strongly about the tyranny of the majority.
That is certainly policy I would support. It is the heart of the Liberal policy, protecting the individual and the rights of the minority. From what I have seen this is an issue where it very much applies, where people at times are hardly responsible for their own action, depending on the conditions under which they were raised. There was a very interesting television

May 2, 1977
Public Opinion on Capital Punishment show about this on the weekend showing where quite often the wrong person is accused of a crime such as murder. My colleagues covered the important aspects of this very well.
The hon. member for Lafontaine-Rosemont (Mr. Lachance) referred to the danger of the referendum to our political system, especially at election time. The hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. MacGuigan) described the lack of legal status of a referendum in Canada, a political process which is certainly more American than British. Therefore it is certainly less Conservative than one would expect from this motion. The hon. member for Northumberland-Miramichi (Mr. Dionne) defended the House debate on the free vote, as I would.
This proposition is rather hypothetical, especially in connection with an election. If on this, then why not on other possible issues for a referendum, or even a plebiscite which really has no binding effect? Why not one on the economy, controls, job creation, business incentive, roles of government? Should the public not have a say there? Why not one on constitutional matters, federal-provincial jurisdiction, repatriation of the Constitution? Why not put that into a referendum at the time of an election, as well as foreign ownership, sovereignty, and other law and order subjects such as gun controls and wiretapping, as well as emotional issues such as abortion and divorce as mentioned by the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville?
If we are going to have a referendum to prevent the tragedy of murder and violence, why not a referendum to ask the Canadian people what kind of commitment they would make to support the government to eliminate these social causes which result in murder, violence, poverty, ignorance, family conflict, child abuse and emotional disorders, which take an innocent baby and create a dangerous criminal, the murderer who, we say, should be disposed of, the one we get upset about?
The hon. member's argument has not persuaded me of the value of the motion. I simply cannot accept it. However, I thank hon. members for the opportunity to address it.

speechtext: The hon. member for Halton has done me the great favour of reading many of the major points I made in my speech when I introduced this motion. Also, he has endorsed almost unanimously all of the points I have made in my speech. My question is, if he agreed with me on most of the major points, why does he not agree to adopting the motion?

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED HOLDING OF NATIONAL REFERENDUM
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the answer is obvious. The quotes I made from the hon. member's speech were quotes which in fact support the position we have taken, abolition. The few points that I do not support are the key points in the motion, the restoration of capital punishment and the very strange use of our political process of referendums, particularly in an election. I was demonstrating that I essentially agree with the hon. member, but he essentially agrees with us. However, he misses the conclusion badly.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED HOLDING OF NATIONAL REFERENDUM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was not my intention to participate in this debate. I still have painful memories of the debate last year in which this House voted to abolish capital punishment. However, I cannot help expressing a few thoughts on the motion before us.
Like many other members of this House, I had hoped we had heard the end of this debate when the House finally took a decision. I voted to retain capital punishment. It was a very difficult personal decision. In the process, I did a poll of my constituents. I had a response substantially in excess of the 10 per cent the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Philbrook) referred to in constituency polls. I think it was in the order of 16 or 17 per cent. About 70 per cent of those who responded indicated that they believed in certain cases capital punishment should be retained.
The process that any member must go through when he knows that there is a firmly held opinion in his constituency on what is a basic moral issue is a very difficult one indeed. I came to the conclusion that for a small number of repeat murderers, the 1 per cent of cases where there is no doubt of guilt of murder in the most brutal circumstances, our institutions are ill equipped to deal with them. It was my opinion that incarceration of 15 or 20 of this kind of prisoner in an institution under long term sentence, with no prospect of parole or release, would create a situation which would be unmanageable in the context of our present institutions.
It was with no small amount of soul searching that I came to the conclusion I had to support retention. In so doing, I was quite surprised at the animosity of the criticism brought on me for doing this. Members of the clergy and a number of others wrote to me saying what a terrible thing I was doing by consulting my constituents.
I was reminded of that old maxim of members being elected to make decisions. That was a quotation from Burke. I understand you can get one from Thomas Payne to the contrary. Depending on the purpose, you always pick the quotation that suits you adequately. In any event, Burke was quoted at that time by those who believed in abolition.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED HOLDING OF NATIONAL REFERENDUM
speechtext: He was defeated next time around.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED HOLDING OF NATIONAL REFERENDUM
speechtext:
The hon. member says that Burke was defeated the next time around. I know what it is to win every second election out of six. That is why I have a sort of uncomfortable feeling looking forward to the next one.
I attempted to search my own conscience and to represent as best I could the people who voted for me. I am aware that the
May 2, 1977

job of a member of parliament is considerably more than rising in one's place just to mirror image an opinion. I am not just a delegate here to go back to a committee in my constituency on every issue that comes up, and ask the committee how I should vote. That is not what I do. But I do try to strike something of a compromise. I believe a democracy means that a majority opinion, firmly held on a basic moral issue, has to be respected. I believe that any elected legislature which flies in the face of that opinion brings a certain degree of contempt upon itself.
I have consulted my constituents on five issues. I went to them on gun control. I got an overwhelming response in favour of tough gun control' laws, but then I represent an urban constituency. Doubtless had I represented a rural constituency the feeling would have gone the other way.
I asked my constituents what they thought of the future form of the government of the National Capital-whether or not it should be a federal district of some sort. I got a very inconclusive response on that issue. The reading I took was that the voters expected me to take the lead and use my best judgment, which is what I shall do on that issue. I may never be called to vote on it in this parliament but I have expressed an opinion on the subject on a number of occasions when appearing before the joint committee of this House and the other place which has been considering the matter.
I polled my constituents again on the question of abortion and I was surprised to find that something like 75 per cent were in favour of much freer abortion laws-I received a 20 per cent response to a householder questionnaire. I could not believe the result so I engaged a firm of professional consultants and asked them about the sampling technique used and, in particular, what kind of response was necessary before one could place any confidence in the results. That group of professional consultants said that if the response was something over 10 per cent I could place some confidence in it, and that a response of 20 per cent deserved a good deal of confidence. They carried out a telephone survey on a carefully selected sample of voters using exactly the same questions, and the response was so close to the response of the householder questionnaire that it was astounding. I can only conclude that there is some validity attached to this method of ascertaining the views of constituents.
This brings me to the next question. To what extent does a legislature reflect on its own decisions? I see the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Friesen) looking at me closely. I did not agree with a decision the House took on capital punishment but I do not intend to pursue any process of consistently reflecting on a decision which has been taken, however much I disagree with it. It seems to me we have an obligation to see how what we are doing now works out.
I intend to watch closely the moves of the Solicitor General (Mr. Fox) toward prison reform. I shall find no difficulty in voting extra money for better staffing of our prisons, the improvement of prison facilities, and the improvement of the
Public Opinion on Capital Punishment parole system. I shall await with a great deal of interest the report of the committee which has been inquiring into the state of our prisons. They have been looking at institutions on the west coast, in the United States and elsewher^ examining different concepts of running such institutions, and their work has been most valuable. I know one thing: in too many cases our prisons today are hell holes. They do not rehabilitate the people who live in them, and in far too many instances those who leave them are not fit to go back into society.
Since we have abolished capital punishment, we have an obligation to follow up that decision with decisions designed to make our prisons more manageable and less subject to criticism. If we do not, we should hang our heads in shame.
I do not find the concept of a referendum very pleasing. I do not believe we should rely on a referendum if the purpose is to find out what people think. The Gallup polls tell us that. The polls we conduct in our own constituencies tell us. As people elected to public office we are sensitive to what voters are thinking. We know what views the majority of the people who elect us hold on various issues. What is at stake is whether, in a democratic legislature, we are prepared to allow a majority opinion to operate on the off chance that it might produce satisfactory results. I find it hard to participate in what I believe would be an act of reflection on a decision taken in this place. At an election time, especially, to do so would colour the vote in many of the constituencies though the hon. member probably thinks this would be a good idea.
Moreover, there are many other subjects to which I personally would give a higher priority. The state of the economy is one, and the issue of national unity, whether or not we are to survive as a nation, is another which should be given the very highest priority. It is my hope that when the next election comes, whenever it may be, we shall not see a repetition of the old capital punishment debate. There may come a time at which this House is called upon to consider that issue once more, but I think the period of the next election would be too soon. I personally would like to give parliament and the country a longer period of time to see what the abolition of capital punishment has really meant, and at the appropriate time, if the results are what I think they may well be, it would be proper to reconsider the matter. However, as I said, I cannot support a motion to hold a referendum, or a plebiscite at the time of the next election, feeling, as I do, that the step parliament has taken ought to be observed over a longer period to see whether or not it will produce beneficial results.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Friesen) on his initiative and tenacity in again bringing the issue of capital punishment to the attention of the House of Commons. As a member who voted in favour of the retention of capital punishment I should like to commend him on his persistence.
I wish, however, that he had brought forward, instead of a motion, a bill so we could have debated the substance of the issue. The hon. member would have had my support had he brought forward a bill. Instead, he presents us with a motion in

May 2, 1977
Public Opinion on Capital Punishment continuance of a debate of November 15 of last year; he wants us to endorse the holding of a national referendum so as to ascertain public opinion on the question of capital punishment at the time of the next federal election.
The matter was initially debated on November 15 of last year. The hon. member for Surrey-White Rock drew a very unfortunate conclusion on his part when he stated that I would support his motion. I fully support the remarks made during that debate by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Dionne). But notwithstanding that I voted in favour of retention and lost, as did others who voted for the retention of capital punishment, I believe that the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock is attempting to fight the issue through very colourable means. We retentionists had our day and we lost.
While I am on this point, Mr. Speaker, I should like to discuss the underlying comment of the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock that backbenchers on this side of the House were subject to influence and pressure by the government. Certainly we were subject to influence and pressure by the government-but not the kind of pressure and influence to which hon. members on the other side of the House cynically refer. Members of the government voted for abolition as a government bill. Nobody has suggested that the cabinet did not have to show solidarity on this particular measure. The government, and yes, members from both sides of the House who favoured abolition exerted a great deal of pressure on me, and I am sure other retentionists, to vote with them, and they did so with their argument that abolition is desirable. There was no threat or inducement, as some opposition members have suggested, on the part of any member of the government to influence me or to exert pressure on me to vote for abolition.
I remember very clearly, Mr. Speaker, that immediately following the second reading vote I did a television interview following the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond-Delta (Mr. Reynolds). If my memory serves me correctly, the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond-Delta alleged that the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) had coerced his backbenchers to vote for abolition, otherwise they might not be able to enhance their parliamentary careers by becoming parliamentary secretaries or cabinet ministers. I voted for retention, Mr. Speaker, and the Prime Minister gave me the privilege and honour of serving the present Solicitor General of Canada (Mr. Fox) as his parliamentary secretary.

Hon. members will recall that she also voted for the retention of capital punishment. Therefore I say to the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock, so much for this myth

The hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. Mac-Guigan) has, I think, very eloquently stated his reasons against a national referendum.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED HOLDING OF NATIONAL REFERENDUM
speechtext:
I will add only a few words to the excellent dissertation of the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville, a very learned member. I said that the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock is using colourable means to fight the issue of capital punishment because the hon. member is attempting to alter our whole parliamentary system of government merely because we retentionists lost. Blacks Law Dictionary defines "referendum" as follows:
In the modern constitutional law of Switzerland and elsewhere, a method of submitting an important legislative measure to a direct vote of the whole people ... Plebiscite: Initiative. Right reserved to the people to adopt or reject any act or measure which has been passed by a legislative body, and which, in most cases, would without action on the part of the electors become a law.
I noted with great interest that the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock deliberately had to use the verbiage "referendum", not "plebiscite", because our parliamentary system of government does grant the right of reserving to the people any act or measure which has been passed by a legislative body and which in most cases would, without action on the part of the electors, become a law. A referendum, in the way the motion is presently drafted, would require subsequent legislative action. What the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock really wants is a plebiscite, which is a non-binding expression of national opinion.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED HOLDING OF NATIONAL REFERENDUM
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED HOLDING OF NATIONAL REFERENDUM
speechtext:
Yes, because you have to come back to the House of Commons. Assuming that the people wanted a referendum and they expressed their desire for capital punishment, we would then have to change the law. It is important to note that Blacks Law Dictionary defines a plebiscite as follows, and I
May 2, 1977

draw this definition to the attention of the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock:
In modern constitutional law, the name "plebiscite" has been given to a vote of the entire people, (that is, the aggregate of the enfranchised individuals composing a state or nation,) expressing their choice for or against a proposed law or enactment, submitted to them, and which, if adopted, will work a radical change in the constitution, or which is beyond the powers of the regular legislative body. The proceeding is extraordinary, and is generally revolutionary in its character; an example of which may be seen in the plebiscites submitted to the French people by Louis Napoleon, whereby the Second Empire was established. But the principle of the plebiscite has been incorporated in the modern Swiss constitution, (under the name of "referendum",) by which a revision of the constitution must be undertaken when demanded by the vote of fifty thousand Swiss citizens.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the time of the adjournment at five o'clock I was in effect showing that the tourist industry in the south shore area could take considerable expansion provided we have the help of both federal and provincial governments to offer the necessary services, communication services between the south shore and the islands within the St. Lawrence, hostelry services, development of a marina as well as a shelter for small fishing and pleasure boats. The geographical location readily lends itself to those facilities, and no matter whether visitors come from Quebec or outside of Quebec if they were informed that they can leave their fishing or pleasure boats under shelter in that area of the river I do think that that would be likely to boost further the tourist industry in our area which would be a considerable contribution to create jobs and conserve the public interest for our area.
Improvement Loans
Mr. Speaker, the people in our area want to survive. They want to live also, not just keep alive. They want to live in a secure environment. The businesses located there provide the population with good services and deserve all our consideration. We have all sorts of businesses there which contribute precisely to creating jobs and helping people get incomes allowing them to live in that area instead of being forced to expatriate themselves and go and live in large centres, and when they have lost their jobs those people go on social welfare or still live for a few weeks on unemployment insurance benefits.
So we must do everything, whatever the area in which members reside, it is in the interest of all that the whole of Canada be developed to offer people jobs so they can earn their living honourably, live off their own efforts. I do think that only at that condition will Canada be able to remain a strong, united country which would be liked by all its inhabitants, irrespective of their language or their culture. I consider we have a vast territory, that it is possible for a very great number of people to live in it, not as enemies but as people liking one another and with the same ideal-making that great Canada an area pleasant to live in in harmony.
As for me, I did not have the chance to learn the intricate subtleties of another language. My colleagues in the House-I am not asking to be excused, it is not that at all-will understand easily that I did not have this chance and in turn, I understand that there are Canadians who have lived in other regions of our country and have not had the chance to learn another language. I can understand them and especially in committee in the House I am aware that we are closer to one another. We try to understand one another, to see the problems of others, to appreciate better any possible solution. This is how I see Canada.
As a family man I was not financially able to give my children all I wished for them. But that does not mean I did not understand them. I asked them: "In turn, you must try to complete what I was not able to do and in so doing, we will grow as a family, establish ourselves and be recognized in a geographical environment." That is how I see Canada, Mr. Speaker, and that is why I am pleading so strongly tonight, as I did this afternoon, for the south shore area. I was ... I hesitate to use the word. I will refrain so as not to displease anyone but in any case, a few weeks ago when I asked a minister in the House if there were any projects to help the regional development of the south shore, he asked me: Where exactly is the south shore; what does it encompass? Mr. Speaker, it bitterly breaks my heart when I think that the south shore is one of the oldest regions of our country.
You only need to know a bit of history, to know where the St. Lawrence River is situated. South of the St. Lawrence, the region that lies between the river and the American border, that is the south shore. We want to ensure that our fellow Canadians who live there can lead normal lives, that our industries, our natural resources are developed, that our small

May 2, 1977
Improvement Loans
businesses carry on, survive and provide work for our children who are still in junior colleges and high schools. We teach them trades, all sorts of things to enable them to serve Canada better while earning a living. This is what we call the south shore and I would like to ensure that this region has the same advantages as all other parts of Canada. It does not matter whether they are English or French-speaking. We should first of all be involved Canadians. If we strive in this way, we will promote Canadian unity, not by great speeches but by our achievements. I appeal to the responsible members of the Quebec Cabinet and ask that they submit a program to the federal government, that is to the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, so that under the federal-provincial agreements the latter may submit a specific project for the development of the South Shore.
We have the St. Lawrence River. We have the islands. We have the South Shore. There are possibilities for a natural touristic development. The Americans keep coming back every fall to do a little white goose, duck and bustard hunting. I know what I am talking about because my home is down by the river. They keep asking us how soon we expect to have means of communications? Whether one may get across at any time of the day or night. Well, no, one has to wait for high tide, one has to wait until mother nature gives us a chance to get across. Are there any accommodations or hotels where one may stay in the meantime? Of course we have, but not very many.
Under this proposal, which should be submitted to the federal government, we might conclude an agreement for touristic growth in the area, to develop better communications, to build piers and highways that would enable the Montmagny region to radiate as the capital of the south shore region. All this progress might enable us to develop our natural resources, services, tourism industry in a profitable way which would bring about stability in the area. Instead of seeing our youth, our sons and daughters obliged to leave the region to go and work in Montreal or Toronto, we could use them to our advantage in our region, and they would help expand this industry and bring about economic stability in this country. Our region would play a role in the settlement of economic problems instead of contributing to increase the number of unemployed.
Mr. Speaker, this is the appeal I want to make tonight to those ministers who are now listening to me. I do so with the generosity and the heart of a responsible individual who wants to work not only for the welfare of his environment but also for those of both his province and the whole country.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the bill before us has led me to make all these remarks because it deals with fisheries, small business, which involves many sectors, and farming which is the main industry in my region.
To conclude, I wish the government would hear my appeal and I ask most sincerely that an amendment be brought to the bill so that interest rates be as low as possible and small business can get loans at interest rates which are in line with regional opportunities, and so that, all together we could really

develop this region which, with the rest of the country, could bring about security and welfare for all Canadians.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE LOANS TO $75,000 FOR IMPROVEMENT OF FARMS, BUSINESSES OR FISHERIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I wish to thank the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert) for his remarks relating to Canadian unity. We, as Canadians, suffer a lot from this effort aimed at dividing the country and the remarks I hear from the south shore of the province of Quebec prompt me to carry this message in my part of the country as well.

My remarks this evening, having thanked the hon. member for Bellechasse, will carry on from some remarks made by the hon. member for Huron-Middlesex (Mr. McKinley) this afternoon, particularly when he referred to the attitude of bankers toward the possibilities under the three acts, the Small Businesses Loans Act, the Farm Improvement Loans Act, and the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act, because it has been my experience that bankers fail to recognize the importance of these acts.
My remarks will be confined entirely to the fishing sector. As expressed by the hon. member for Huron-Middlesex this afternoon, the attitude of the bankers was that there was no money for loans in these areas, whether it be for small business, agriculture or fisheries, but then on reconsideration they said that provided these people brought them the rest of their banking business, fine. To my way of thinking there ought to be something in this law which would encourage the banks to take a more positive attitude. The fishermen themselves have complained about this attitude of the banks.
At the week end members of the Progressive Conservative British Columbia caucus held a meeting in Vancouver. Representations were made to us by a number of fishing organizations, one being the Fishing Vessel Owners' Association of British Columbia. That association presented a comprehensive brief. I was not aware at that time that I would be rising to discuss this bill this evening. However, the following comment in the brief bears out entirely what the hon. member said this afternoon:
... banks have tended to shy away from fish boat financing except for shortterm, high interest loans .. .
This, of course, does not help fishermen at all. These loans are not loans in the ordinary sense. They are guarantees of loans. It is a no-risk proposition. The bank has nothing to lose here. If it guarantees the loan, it will be repaid. Granted, it is a very small amount, but I will come back to that in a moment. It must be underlined that these are guarantees of loans, and therefore the element of risk is minimized, if not indeed completely eliminated. It is clear to me that the fishermen of this country suffer from a number of impediments to their development. They are uncertain as to the future, partly because of inflation, and partly because of the changing policies of this government with respect to fisheries.

Just a few months ago on the west coast, a week or so before the fisheries were to open, it was proposed that fishermen should be required to choose whether they want to fish the inside waters of Vancouver Island or the outside waters. This was in anticipation of a further requirement that they choose the gear with which they fish, whether it be trollers, gillnetters or seiners. That is what the press release indicated, all in the interest of conservation, without anything being done about enhancement.
Be that as it may, these are some of the uncertainties facing fishermen on the west coast, and I am sure they face fishermen on the east coast as well. Fishermen also face uncertainty about financing their boats. I will come to the cost of boats these days. Fishermen are also uncertain about financing their gear and the chilling equipment they need to keep their fish fresh. These are elements within the bill which deserve wider publicity. They deserve to be recognized by the banks and, as I said earlier, I feel that the banks should somehow be encouraged to meet the requirements of the fishermen. In the past the banks have largely ignored this particular act.
The same brief from which I quoted earlier mentions that there is very little incentive for the private vessel owner who upgrades his fish holding facilities at his own expense but is not compensated for the higher quality of his product. There is little incentive for fishermen to take advantage of the fish-chilling subsidy program, which is partly subsidy and partly loans under this act. It is really remarkable that so few banks seem to be aware of what facilities might be financed under this legislation.
It is right and proper to ask why the banks should be required to be more responsive to fishermen's needs. In this context I think it is worth mentioning something about the importance of the fishing industry. I speak only of the fishing industry in British Columbia. Let me put on the record some figures which indicate the importance of the fishing industry in British Columbia. I refer here to a brief presented to the B.C. Progressive Conservative caucus members who met last week end in Vancouver. The wholesale market value of fish products from 1973 to 1975 averaged $222.9 million a year, roughly a quarter of a billion dollars.
I think it is worth referring to another section from the same brief presented by the Pacific Gillnetters Association.
B.C. catch figures for 1972 to 1976 averaged 337.4 million pounds per year.
That is a great heap of fish.
Foreign fleets within our 200 mile limit catch an estimated 108.6 million pounds per year. The total-446 million pounds-is a very important part of the world's source of protein-and yet, according to the Fisheries Service estimates, it is less than one half of the potential sustained yield level of 1 billion pounds per year of this renewable resource in B.C. coastal waters.
In other words, there is a vast potential of fish off the west coast which is not now being caught safely in order to preserve the fisheries, contrary to the recommendation of the fisheries service of this country. In order to catch this amount, obviously the fishermen have to improve their facilities and their ability to catch fish. Mr. Speaker, I wonder if you have any idea how much it costs to build and equip a fishing boat.
Improvement Loans

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE LOANS TO $75,000 FOR IMPROVEMENT OF FARMS, BUSINESSES OR FISHERIES
speechtext:
I will quote some figures from the brief presented by the Gillnetters Association as follows:
Capital and operating costs have skyrocketed the last five years and yet fish prices have not risen as much although when you buy it it may seem that way. As an example, the same gillnetter that was built in 1960, sold in 1971 for $12,000 (no licence value), sold again in 1976 for $60,000, ($40,000 for the boat and $20,000 for the licence) a factor of 5, whereas fish prices, in the same period rose only by a factor of 2.
These are important statistics, and they indicate the problems confronting fishermen in British Columbia.
It is always worth looking at the original act this bill seeks to amend. Section 3 of the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act, found in the Revised Statutes of Canada, chapter F-22, page 3231, provides for guaranteed loans. It says that the minister shall, subject to this act, pay to a lender the amount of loss sustained by it as a result of a loan made to a fisherman. The section lists the purposes for which a loan may be made. They include the purchase of construction of a fishing vessel; the purchase or construction of fishing equipment; the major repair or major overhaul of a fishing vessel or its hull, superstructure or engine; or the purchase or construction of a shore installation. The latter purpose relates to the chilling facilities mentioned earlier. The act sets out purposes or areas with respect to which the bank may provide assistance in financing a fisherman's enterprise.
As has been noted earlier, the present day fisherman is a small businessman. For example, the gillnetter has changed in the last 50 years from a labourer catching fish with processor-company owned boats and gear to an independent businessman with significant investment and high operating costs.
As I said, the act guarantees loans negotiated for the purchase or construction of a fishing vessel or fishing equipment, for major repairs and overhauls, and for the purchase and construction of shore installations. And what amounts of money are involved in these guaranteed loans? In 1955, when the original act was passed, the maximum guaranteed loan was $25,000. In 1974 the act was amended, raising loan limits to $50,000. Now, three years later, those loan limits are once more to be raised to $75,000. Why has the limit been raised from $50,000 to $75,000? Obviously the increase does no more than take into account the incidence of the inflation we have suffered since 1974. The inflation factor of 50 per cent, which is about the amount of inflation we have experienced in the last three years, is reflected in this amendment.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE LOANS TO $75,000 FOR IMPROVEMENT OF FARMS, BUSINESSES OR FISHERIES
speechtext:
Let me quote again from the brief submitted by the Fishing Vessel Owners Association of British Columbia in 1975. Please remember that when the brief was submitted the loan ceiling was $50,000. They said at that time:
The Fisheries Improvement Loan Program, with a $50,000 maximum is currently directed toward new boat purchases. In an industry where a Fisherman can own a $500,000 boat and $100,000 worth of gear, this is an insignificant amount.
Clearly, even $75,000 is insignificant in this context. I continue quoting:
The program should be extended in order to offer the Fisherman a realistic alternative to company indebtedness.
At present fishermen are indebted to companies. Our fishermen are obliged to rent or lease their boats from the processor, or from the processing company. Therefore their sales are controlled. The brief goes on to say that if we are to correct the situation we must raise the loan limit to something like $250,000, which is far above $75,000. We could thereby give fishermen the option of refinancing their existing debts or upgrading existing vessels. Those were the views of the Fishing Vessel Owners Association on the west coast.
We are not going to delay unduly passage of this bill, but I do say that it is worth putting some facts on record. Let me summarize. The fisherman is a small businessman, if one can consider an operation requiring a $500,000 investment in a boat and $100,000 in equipment as a small business. Certainly it is a bigger business than I could become involved in if I could borrow from the bank only $75,000. Therefore when we speak of a small business in this context we are speaking of one requiring capital investment of $600,000. Further, fishermen must brave the elements and find markets. Theirs is an important business. Is it any wonder our fishermen are concerned? They have their contribution to make to the economy, and are ready to make it. They want to earn a living, a decent living, but their difficulty is in Financing, that is, in updating or buying new equipment for their operation.
The licensing system has introduced an element of uncertainty in this area, but I had better not deal with that subject at the moment. Some fishermen have had to equip their boats with a second type of gear. If they were gillnetters they have had to put on troll equipment, because when they are not gillnetting, they can troll. Now some attempts are being made to curtail that kind of operation.
It is strange that three years ago, in 1974, the amendment to the act increased the maximum permissible guaranteed loan from $25,000 to $50,000 and now, three years later, we are raising that limit once more to $75,000. Mr. Speaker, our Fishermen are not asking to be Financed or supported for all time. They will pay the money back, but they feel, because of the hundreds of thousands of dollars they must spend, that they should be given greater encouragement for the contribution they want to make to the economy and to feeding the world.
