speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE LOANS TO $75,000 FOR IMPROVEMENT OF FARMS, BUSINESSES OR FISHERIES
speechtext:
Let me turn for five minutes to some of the criticisms that have been made of this piece of legislation. The hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) said that in 1975, the year that he picked, only ten loans were made to farmers in Newfoundland under the Farm Improvement Loans Act, while in the country as a whole there were 30,000 loans. To impress the folks back home, he asked why the lending was so low in Newfoundland.
Improvement Loans
I looked at some of the figures with regard to loans made to farmers in Newfoundland. There are 195,000 commercial farms in Canada. Two hundred of them are in Newfoundland.
In other words, if you look at the number of farms there are in Newfoundland compared to the number of commercial farms there are in the country, Newfoundland is getting more than its share. That was supposed to be an argument against. It is one of the reasons why this parliament has to waste its time hour after hour in opposition to a bill which members opposite agree with in principle.
Many members opposite spoke about the definition of a small business. They said that a million dollars is too low a ceiling for annual gross revenue of an eligible small business, and it should be raised to $1,500,000. That is an increase of 50 per cent. I have not done any research into the viability of an enterprise of $1 million and $1.5 million of annual gross revenues, but listen to this. If you take the $1 million limit which the government has proposed in this legislation, it covers 95 per cent of all of the corporations, partnerships, and sole proprietorships in this country.
We picked a definition for small business that covers 95 per cent of the enterprises in Canada. Ninety-five per cent will benefit from this legislation. Possibly members opposite would like Bell Canada to qualify for a loan under the Small Businesses Loans Act. If so, let us hear about it in committee. Let us hear which businesses are cut out by the $1 million limit, and which should be included under a limit that might go to $1.5 million. But what the heck, we are covering 95 per cent of them under this proposal. We are increasing it 50 per cent from what it is now. Let us get on with it and settle it.
The next point raised was the $75,000 limit which is proposed in this legislation. They say that is inadequate as the maximum loan amount. It is presently $50,000. We are proposing a mere 50 per cent increase. Maybe the opposition does have a point; maybe the ceiling should be higher. Maybe this is something that should be looked at it in committee. However, when we are looking at in committee, one of the statistics that ought to be looked at is that the average loan made under this act with the present $50,000 limit is $16,000. Under the Farm Improvement Loans Act, the average loan is $7,500. The average under the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act was $14,000.
When you look at figures for the average loans of $16,000, $14,000, and $7,500, it becomes obvious that the suggestion that the limit ought to be raised from $50,000 beyond $75,000, which we propose, is a stalling tactic. It is a ceiling which is not of interest to very many, if any, members of the business community. If the majority of loans are made at figures like this, is it worth the time of this House to argue that the ceiling proposed by the government, 50 per cent higher than the present ceiling and nearly 500 per cent higher than the average loan, ought to be made even higher than that?
A couple of members opposite have suggested that there ought to be more government participation in the operation of this act. It has been suggested that before a loan can be obtained from an approved lender, government officials ought

May 2, 1977
Improvement Loans
to appraise the loan and make a decision with regard to it in advance. That is a very well meaning suggestion. It gets to the point that a bank might be prejudiced against a particular customer while an official reviewing the matter might, by his intervention, prevent that from happening. However, that must happen in only a very small percentage of the cases. There are 166 lenders who can make these loans.
Looking at that proposal, I feel that it just adds red tape to the procedure. It delays the businessman. It obliges him not only to go to a lender but to stop on the way at a new government office, where new bureaucrats go through more paperwork. I am willing to consider the suggestion in the Finance Committee, of which I am a member, but I do not believe it is one which will commend itself to the average businessmen who might want to take advantage of the act.
Finally, there is a criticism that more lenders should be authorized under the act to make loans. As I said a few moments ago, 166 institutions are presently designated. But it is virtually an open category, not a closed list. As many institutions as possible ought to be recognized. We should bear in mind, though, that a lender can abuse his recognition under the act and that once a loan is granted it is guaranteed by the Canadian taxpayer. In these circumstances we want to make sure that the lenders are the kind of people who will take a critical look at the circumstances on which a loan is based.
This is not a program designed to give out subsidies; that is not what those engaged in small enterprises are seeking. What they have in mind is loans, and it is not unreasonable, in the interest of the taxpayer, for the government to satisfy itself that the lenders will screen these transactions carefully to make sure that the money loaned is likely to be repaid.
I might point out that different criteria for institutional approval are used in different parts of the country. When an applicant lives in an area which is not well served by financial institutions the requirement for eligibility is not so strict. I myself would like to see more financial institutions involved, but the important thing to remember is that we have legislation here which will broaden and move the program forward. It is not the kind of legislation which hon. members ought to delay by making one 40-minute speech after another.
I shall sit down at this point, without having taken half my 40 minutes. I have tried to make a useful contribution to the debate, and I urge hon. members as they rise from the benches opposite to make the comments they have in mind in the spirit that this is legislation of which all parties approve. Let them not take all the time available to them. Let us pass the bill along and get on with other business.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE LOANS TO $75,000 FOR IMPROVEMENT OF FARMS, BUSINESSES OR FISHERIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is one point on which I agree with the hon. member who just resumed his seat, namely, that speeches to be immortal need not be eternal. I shall not take very long to make my points. I shall not take as long as the hon. member has just taken. He spent several minutes giving us a lecture on how to

conduct our business. It seems to me the House is a debating forum in which we put forward our views and the views of those we represent. I rise to speak, as is my right, because I am interested in the Farm Improvement Loans Act. I have made use of that legislation over the years and I believe there are some defects in it. I want to use this opportunity to call attention to those defects.
We are talking about the Farm Improvement Loans Act, the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act, and the Small Businesses Improvement Loans Act. The proposal is to increase the allowable maximum from $50,000 to $75,000, and the definition of "small business" is broadened. We are also extending the period in which this legislation is to operate to June 30, 1980.
The hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan) mentioned some reasons for supporting the bill, including the need to increase the maximum loan to $75,000. Mr. Speaker, that is merely keeping up with inflation. It is only common sense that this should be done. I do not think the government can take any credit for simply keeping up with the times, although it might be something of a new experience for it. It is a fact, for instance, that the cost of farm machinery has more than doubled in recent years. The cost of fertilizer and of all the other items necessary to a farmer has similarly increased, so the loan ceiling must be raised if the money is to be used for the purposes we have in mind.
Then, too, it is important that "small business" be redefined. This segment of society is, after all, the backbone of the economy and the biggest user of this kind of credit. Small business, in the aggregate, probably employs as many people as do our larger corporations. An expansion of small business means the creation of more jobs. One point which should be recognized by the government and by the banks is that many of these loans may involve risk capital which cannot be secured from another source. The banks run only a small risk in making these loans because, of course, the money is guaranteed by the government. The legislation should naturally concern itself, then, with the provision of risk capital. These changes are long overdue.
Now for some criticism. There is no mention in the bill of what the interest rate is likely to be, though this is a matter of first importance, as it is to other sections of the economy, the construction industry, for example, whose slowness in expanding is at least partly due to the exorbitant interest rates which are demanded. It seems to me it would not be unreasonable to ask that the banks make loans under this act at least at the prime rate, a rate which it is most difficult to get, as anyone who has ever applied for one of these loans will tell you. I should like to see a clause here to implement a proposal that the interest rate to be charged for loans under these acts would be the prime rate.
I have a second criticism. There must be some way of putting pressure on the banks to make loans, and to make loans of a sufficient size to achieve the purpose for which they are sought. It is true a ceiling exists, but the lenders will not go anywhere near this ceiling in many cases; it is hard to convince
May 2, 1977

them that sums of a certain size are necessary to do the job that is required. The interest rate no doubt has a bearing on this reluctance. A bank can get a better return by lending money on a demand note, so it is simply not good business for it to lend money under the legislation we are considering. This is one of the problems we face.
Surely one would think a government guarantee would be sufficient incentive for a bank to make a loan at a lower rate of interest, but events have proven that it is not so. It has always seemed to me that a carrot is better than a stick when you are trying to get someone to do what you want him to do, but evidently in this case the carrot is not big enough. I suggest all three acts should have some mechanism which would put pressure on banks to grant loans.
Under the Farm Credit Corporation Act a farmer applies for a loan to the Farm Credit Corporation, which appraises his case. If the corporation refuses the loan, the farmer has the right to appeal the ruling of the corporation to a review board. The appeal board is made up of successful farmers who know what farming is all about, what loans are reasonable, and they assess the ability of the farmer to repay. It seems to me that a mechanism like this should be found so that people who are refused loans can seek redress. I think this is long overdue and is a just criticism which the government should consider.
Let me give the House some examples of people who have been refused loans. I am sure all hon. members have known of people who have endeavoured to get loans under these acts, have been refused, and consequently have gone to see their member, who has then interceded on their behalf. Two instances come to my mind, and these have to do with the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act. I have a Lake Erie freshwater fishery based on Port Dover, and two men who came to my attention were William C. Misener of R. R. No. 3, Port Dover and Frank G. Bravener, also of Port Dover. Their applications were turned down and they came to me to talk it over. I thought that their requests were reasonable on the basis of what they said, and what I understood to be fair, and so I wrote to the then minister of finance, the Hon. John Turner. My letter read as follows:
Many farmers and fishermen have come to me over the past several months complaining about their inability to obtain loans from their banker under the Farm Improvement Loans Act and/or the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act.
Many of these people have sound business proposals but are refused loans for rather trivial reasons. I have explained the fact that the banker makes the final decision in all these cases. Sometimes I feel it is due to the fact that the bank receives greater interest on its own loans than on those guaranteed by the government.
This letter is to strongly urge that your department consider some method of putting pressure on bankers to approve loans where the credit rating and the proposed project are sound.
My most recent request came from Mr. Wm. C. Misener of R. R. No. 3, Port Dover, Ontario, who has been a fisherman all his life and now has the opportunity to purchase the boat presently owned by his employer. There is no doubt about this man's ability to carry such a loan and to repay on reasonable terms.
Improvement Loans
I would appreciate it if your officials would reply directly to Mr. Misener and, if possible, indicate any means by which he might qualify for the loan he is seeking.
This case happened to turn out all right. Evidently the director of the guaranteed loans branch of the Department of Finance did contact the bank in question and the man got his loan, so there was a happy conclusion. But I submit that no member should have to intercede on behalf of this kind of person. As I suggested a few moments ago, an appeal procedure might be the remedy in such cases.
The acts which are to be amended by Bill C-48 do much to assist the groups referred to in the acts to obtain credit to expand their operations, despite the shortcomings that I have mentioned. Tobacco farmers whom I represent in large numbers make great use of the Farm Improvement Loans Act. They also have need for other assistance, and just recently they discussed with the minister the possibility of entering into serious negotiations in regard to implementing a two price system for tobacco. The Ontario Flue-cured Tobacco Growers Marketing Board feel it is imperative that we establish a two-price system similar to that now in place for the export of wheat. Tobacco quotas have been cut 50 per cent on average over the last few years.
I think most hon. members know that nearly $1 billion accrues to governments at all levels as a result of taxation on tobacco and tobacco products. To be efficient we must produce up to 100 per cent, and to do this we must export. If the minister were to take a look at establishing a two-price system for this very important product in our economy, we would be able to sell all our product. The result would be a more prosperous local economy, more funds in the federal treasury, a substantial increase in exports, and an improvement in the balance of trade deficit. Following this there would be further need for loans under the Farm Improvement Loans Act.
Despite all of the shortcomings I have mentioned, I hope that the minister who is piloting this bill through the House, as well as the member who was so critical of any suggestions that we make, will take note of some of the positive proposals that we have made for improving this legislation. However, we do intend to support Bill C-48, and we will see that we get some amendments proposed in committee.

speechtext:
I should like to make a few comments on this bill based on my knowledge of small business and the relationship of a small businessman to his banker. I feel that if we

May 2, 1977
Improvement Loans
want to examine why this program is not growing we should take a look at the third person in the arrangement. There is the small businessman, there is the government, but what about the banker?
I spent some time during the last few days interviewing and telephoning people on the banking side who have had experience of these loans to find out what they thought about them, and I was quite interested to hear what they had to say in regard to limits and in regard to restrictions. The bank managers I called asked me who had dreamt up the exciting and dramatic increase from $50,000 to $75,000. Somebody in the government must like tidy arithmetic. Banks which are growing and which are really giving excellent service to their clients tell me that their loan limit is $250,000. I guess our brothers across the way think that $75,000 is just what is needed. A small baker today who wants to start up a small business on main street could not even get his dough mixed with $75,000; it takes at least $150,000 to even bake at all.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE LOANS TO $75,000 FOR IMPROVEMENT OF FARMS, BUSINESSES OR FISHERIES
speechtext: It depends what kind of dough you want!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE LOANS TO $75,000 FOR IMPROVEMENT OF FARMS, BUSINESSES OR FISHERIES
speechtext:
Not some of the "crummy" kind. One banker last week told me that he had lent money for a ditching machine to lay tile, and this one machine cost $75,000. I would have to say to the Minister of State (Small Business) (Mr. Marchand) that the tombstone which will mark the grave of his ministry will be inscribed "Small is Beautiful" unless he becomes more realistic about the financial needs of small business, and wakes up the finance department to establish adequate levels of loans for this part of the community.
Something else the bankers mentioned to me was the amount of red tape. I should like to put on the record some of the comments that came to me during the last few days: "I can't suffer the pages and pages of instruction"; "We can't be bothered with the paperwork, ours is much simpler"; "It is unattractive because of the many forms". Perhaps we could strike a new 12 cent stamp or put up a statue to the person in the Ministry of Finance who could cut the small loans form in half. I think the small business sector of the community would finance such a venture. In fact I have a sneaking suspicion that the banks would probably underwrite the cost. Cannot you hear the teachers or scout leaders saying to their children as they pass by the statue, "That statue was put up by citizens of the country to the person in the Department of Finance who learned how to cut a form in half'. I can hear these children saying, "Our Hero!"
One bank manager I spoke to told me that he has built two branches on his record of loans, yet in seven years he has granted only one small business loan. The bankers tell me that the prime rate would be fine and this would be excellent, "but for goodness sake, lift the levels and also cut the paperwork." I find only 5,092 loans made last year in a country this size which is crying out for risk capital for the smaller business units.

This act could be another effective tool to create growth, jobs, and wealth. My grandfather had a saying, "Lift the level of the lake and all the canoes float higher." Cut the paperwork, lift the levels, and a lot will float higher.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is a very serious situation when in a country with the resources of Canada we have not done the kind of developing that we ought to have been doing during the past decade. This evening a member of the government party came in and gave a hit and run speech. The hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan) wants to guillotine us in the parliament Chamber itself, knowing full well that if we followed the advice he put forward-to let the legislation go to committee-that all legislation would go through because the government has not made an effective committee system.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE LOANS TO $75,000 FOR IMPROVEMENT OF FARMS, BUSINESSES OR FISHERIES
speechtext:
As the hon. member was speaking he knew full well that in the committee system we simply have a miniature House, with the government in power also practising the guillotine there.
If we were to accept the premise the hon. member for York Centre put forward-that we are wasting our time by speaking in this Chamber-that is a self-admission by government members that they do not listen to the debate on this side of the House. The fact is that if this is to be a chamber of debate, then it must be one not only of speaking but of listening. If there is to be some resolve in all of the members coming from the various parts of this country, then that has to come from the fact that government changes its legislation in light of what it hears.
I am appalled that a member of the government would say that he does not want to hear the voices of so many sectors that are being raised in this Chamber. He talked about the average of varying costs. All I would say to the hon. member for York Centre is: because he goes forward on the assumption of averaging, if he had his head in a firebox and his feet on a block of ice, on the average he would feel pretty good.
Let us turn to the issue of Bill C-48. It is a bill that deals with small businessmen, with farmers, and with fishermen. If we take a look at the very important aspects of small business, we note the need in this country for higher rates of financing and we find out that the amount allocated in the bill itself is so small, a $75,000 maximum, that it will not even buy a decent toot for the tugboats.
When we talk about inland fisheries we are talking about the northern fisheries of this country, those in the territories, in the three prairie provinces and in northern Ontario, and in almost every one of the instances of northern fisheries we are talking about people who are trying to develop a resource quite some distance away from banks and banking institutions. These are people who do not have the opportunity to sit down
May 2, 1977

with a banker to work out loans of any particular merit. They are people who, by their very lifestyle and their nature of living, are not going to get the kind of capital resources they need in order to develop the resources that this country provides. It is very important that we underscore that freshwater fisheries are largely worked by the native groups of this country. The people who presently are bracketed in that category, also known as our highly unemployed people, work in areas of ever-decreasing markets. The native people are largely those who have tried to capitalize in the inland water fishery.
If there is something that we can point out that is absolutely obvious, it is that under the present legislation there is no obligation on banks and banking institutions to lend money. It simply leaves them with the prerogative of lending money only if they chose to do so. If we take a look at the incentives which are naturally associated with banks, obviously their motive is one of profit-making. While we do not fault them for that, the fact of the matter is that they are not going to be lending at low interest rates when they can hold out for higher interest rate loans.
The fact of the matter is that we have to look at a whole rethinking of a new national dream for this country, a kind of dream that begins to project for the Canadian people the opportunity to develop our resources. That is not what is being put forward by this piece of legislation. The limitations that exist therein are of such an extent that we are going to find they are really nothing more than an extension of an old program, except to make up for some of the inflation that the government has brought down upon us. In other words, all they are saying is that they are putting a bill forward to try to cover up some of the mistakes of their past administration. They are saying they have caused inflation and therefore they will add some amendments to the bill that may make it look as though some of that inflation was not there. What it does not do is provide capital to the extent that the people of this country can develop our resources to an even greater degree than at the present time.
If we might take a look at some of the fishing on the Atlantic coastline, I had the privilege this past year of having a meeting with the Hon. Frank Moores, the premier of Newfoundland, and he told me that if Canada could catch and process off the coast of Newfoundland all of the fish that are caught by other countries off that 200-mile limit, Newfoundland would have 17 per cent of Canada's Gross National Product. If you extend that out to all ten provinces and every province had 17 per cent, then Canada would have 170 per cent, or an increase of 70 per cent in our Gross National Product.
It is obvious that something is amiss when a province simply cannot develop its resources to the extent that it ought to be able to do so. I asked the premier what it was that was holding him back. He said that what was holding him back was that they needed $l'/2 billion of capital in order to go ahead.
Take a look at some of the ways we go about job creation in this country, such as LIP, LEAP, Young Canada Works and
Improvement Loans
Canada Works, with people out there shingling roofs and fixing up graveyards. That temporarily stops some of the unemployment but does not give the kind of capital to this nation that is necessary so that we might progress with viable, economic, soundly managed business in order to get away from temporary work projects and all of these ad hoc administratively tied pieces of legislation that fail to develop the country to its fullest potential.
Take a look at Bill C-48. It is just as bad as LIP, LEAP, Young Canada Works and Canada Works. It does nothing more than add on ad hoc administrative problems because it does not take a look at the real needs of the country, nor does it ascertain the real potentials of the country.
Moving from the fishing industry to the farming industry, I would point out that it is simple audacity to talk about loans for farmers when, on the one hand, the increase in the limit is only $25,000 and farm machinery price increases in the past four or five years make that amount seem absolutely insignificant. We have heard the hon. member for York Centre say that they are adding another $25,000 to the limit a person can borrow. Rather than being any chastisement of what this party has been saying, it underscores the fact that the hon. member for York Centre does not know anything about the cost of farm machinery. If he understood that and how much it has increased during this past four to five years, then he would recognize full well that an increase to a $75,000 maximum loan in no way permits a person to enter into a farming enterprise today.
What we find perhaps even more distressing is the fact that Bill C-48 comes at a time when the government, through its mismanagement, perhaps contrived mismanagement, has forced us into a situation where beef producers are going into their fourth year of operating at a loss. It all started when the government, in its lack of wisdom, put forward the LIFT program which was supposed to take cultivated land out of production and put it into grassland. What the programs did in effect was to increase the number of breeding cows and heifers to the extent that in an 18 month period the number of breeding cattle in Canada increased by 45 per cent. The reason for that is so obvious. When you increase grassland in production, you increase cattle production, because you must recognize that people do not eat grass, pigs do not eat grass nor do chickens eat grass-it is cattle that eat grass.
The LIFT program would have been far better named had it been called the goof program. What it did was to lift farmers and ranchers into bankruptcy. For four years farmers have been going to the bank to borrow capital to pay the debts of the previous year. The government tries to take some credit for the fact that it has increased the maximum amount that can be borrowed by $25,000 when the fact that money must be borrowed has been caused by the government's mismanagement.
I cannot leave this subject without mentioning once again that not only has the government failed in not knowing what

May 2, 1977
Improvement Loans
would happen when grassland is increased and subsequently beef production is increased, but the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) has failed miserably in his GATT negotiations and lost the battle with the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Chretien). What was the result of that? It is there before all Canadians to see. The answer is simple.
We lost in the trade negotiations and therefore Canada now imports into the country a record amount of beef and veal in boneless cuts from Australia and New Zealand at a time of domestic overproduction in Canada. That is the situation in which the government has the audacity to pretend that it is making a significant contribution to the farm people. Then, after several years of pressure from the opposition parties, the Minister of Agriculture came forward to say he would impose quotas on Oceanic beef coming to Canada. However, a week ago I was alarmed to find out that although there is a quota, what has happened in effect in the first twelve weeks of 1977 is that 42 per cent of that quota has been used up. That means that as soon as all the quota is used up, the price of cattle will start to rise.
As stated not only by the Canadian Cattlemen's Association but by the cattle breeders south of the border, there will be an outcry from consumer markets in this country and the government will react by bringing in quotas and establishing a cheap food policy. The policy the government has been operating under is to try to extend to Canada a cheap food policy without regard for the fact that it is destroying a viable beef producing industry simply for the sake of gaining votes in another part of the country.
I should underscore the fact that the Minister of Agriculture continues his imposition of marketing boards on farmers even though that is not their wish, and even though the province of Manitoba opposed it in a referendum by 77 per cent. So when we take a look at the kinds of loans they are extending and we know that while they have increased by some 25 per cent, I submit the government would do far more for the producing industry if it took a look at the blue book on import quotas in the past year and if it recognized that in honey, dairy products, fruits and vegetables, beef, pork, hams, and so on, although the tariff reduction has been a minimum 5 per cent, on the average it has been 15 per cent on those products.
Canada, which was once a net exporter of pork, is now a net importer of that product. We were once a net exporter of beef, now we import beef. Canada has become a net importer of food, all because the government has totally destroyed our agricultural marketing system. We should recognize that we will not patch up the damage which the government has done by simply lifting the ceiling on the amount that a farmer can borrow, because in fact he is going broke. What we will have to do is to do something about the marketing of our products. If there is anything that Canada is failing to do in the producer industry, in forestry, fisheries, small businesses and farming, it is the failure to sell our products on the international markets.
What should be clear, especially to those in the farming industry, is that the approach which the government is taking

to selling our products is to put them on the shelf and hope that a buyer will come forward. There is no such thing as an aggressive salesmanship team in Canada which would sell our products. If the government undertook to adopt an aggressive sales policy, and recognized the fact that four fifths of the world suffers from malnutrition and that 12,000 children a day under the age of five die of starvation, as well as the fact that agricultural products are the products highest in demand anywhere in the world, then farmers should be able to make it on their own.
The role of the government is in research and marketing. It is failing to get our products into international markets and therefore it is letting industry down. Coming along with catch-up, ad hoc policies implying "we will lend you money because you are going into debt" will,not help the farmers because they do not believe that kind of guff. Increasing loans to $75,000 does not compensate for the inflation that has taken place in the agricultural industry.
I suggest there are a couple of areas where the government could help the agricultural industry if it were serious about doing so. There are some old tariff laws which, although minor, affect a few people. Traditionally, farm machinery coming from the United States has been coming in free of tariff. Let us take, for example, farm wagons. The reason there is no import reduction on them is that wagons were used for bringing in equipment, labelled products, from the railway stations, stores, garages and villages. Today wagons are no longer used for the purpose. Instead, trucks are used for that purpose. But if you bring in separately four inch harvesters with an option on the different kinds of undercarriages, there is a tariff attached.
What is more important, if the government wanted to do something for the agricultural industry it would reduce the tariff to the non-profit co-ops, such as seed cleaning plants. Every time they want to bring in equipment from the U.S. to Canada they are not allowed the same exemptions as farmers in general receive. Yet, because of the high cost of farming in the country today, many farmers get together and form a co-operative, with larger pieces of machinery, seed cleaning plants, large tractors and so forth. As soon as they form into a non-profit co-operative, they no longer get those tariff benefits. If the government is sincere in listening, as I hope the minister is this evening, this is one area where he could make an effective addition to the amendments that are put forward.
I do not believe the government ought to be making large contributions to farmers' net income in a direct way, but an analysis of what is happening around the world shows some very startling and interesting data in relation to Canada's role in assisting farmers. Government support to farmers' net income in Great Britain amounts to 67 per cent, in France 50 per cent, in the United States 17 per cent, and in Canada 1.7 per cent. I do not believe it ought to be the role of the government to become involved in farmers' income in a direct way, but surely it ought to be involved in research and
May 2, 1977

marketing to a greater extent than the negligible extent it has been in past years. We fail to sell our products in the international market place. There is no product in the world for which there is a greater need than food. Canada only contributes 1.7 per cent to farmers' net income, and I think that says something about our marketing system and something about the infinitely small amount of money being put toward research in this country.
Before I conclude I would like to refer to another area where I believe the government, if it wanted to help small business and if it were sincere in its effort, could help. Government red tape is a stumbling block to the development of business. An imaginative concept is the idea of farming musk oxen. The meat of the musk ox has medical value. It is used in connection with heart care. Musk ox meat has a low cholesterol content. Doctors would like to have musk ox meat available for that reason. The oviat, while like the wool of sheep, is of much more value than wool. It is stronger in its tensile strength and warmer because of the characteristics of the oviat. Nevertheless, we note that the production of musk oxen is restricted to the northern territories, and musk oxen are not allowed to come into southern Canada unless a fee of $10,500 is paid just to start up some kind of research on southern Canada.
The musk ox grazes on brushland. It makes use of what we would call marginally low class soil regions. After numerous attempts with various departments all we meet is frustration and lack of success in trying to develop a whole new industry. I might add that the Montreal textile market is willing to pay as much as $9 a pound for the oviat. We find that there is a market for the meat, but the government nevertheless takes the view that it will not allow people to bring that kind of animal into southern Canada.
In spite of efforts by members of parliament the government will not get involved with veterinary research or with marketing because of red tape and stumbling blocks, but Canada gives 16 musk oxen to the Russians so that the Russians can start a farming operation. Recently Sweden bought musk oxen in from Norway. Other countries are getting into this. I use this example to demonstrate that people with imagination who want to develop this country run into stumbling blocks, while we continue with the kind of resources we have had in the past, and the government simply introduces programs to patch up its own inflationary mistakes. This country is filled with human resources. There are people to build a big and better Canada, but because of the government's restrictive attitude on many fronts, Canadian incentive is being destroyed, and the situation is such that we cannot move forward to develop to the extent we ought.
With regard to Bill C-48, the total assets of the banking industry of Canada amount to about $130 billion. It takes just a little bit of mathematics to come to the conclusion that this bill will cover only .4 per cent of the total banking operation in Canada and that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) has failed in his responsibility.
The Government of Canada is lending money to Cuba at the rate of 3 per cent. The government fails to recognize that while
Improvement Loans
we can get money from the banks at 12 per cent, it is in essence saying that Canadians with imagination have to pay 9.5 per cent, but that it will give loans to Cuba at 3 per cent. I think it is a shame that the government cannot recognize the need for capitalizing this country and for allowing people's imagination and incentives to go forward and to develop a progressive country.
The hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Darling) said that small businesses in Canada provide more than 55 per cent of the jobs in this country. They account for more than 50 per cent of the dollar value of business conducted in our country, and that is no small amount. He said that, taken as an economic unit, the small business community is the single most important economic community in our country. It is on that note that I wish to conclude.
Small businesses are the economic backbone of this nation. On almost every front-the amount of capital which is being made available, banking institutions lending money, government restrictions on putting money into the lending market, government destruction of people's imagination in such enterprises as farming musk oxen-it is high time the government opened up and trusted Canadians because it is small business people who will develop this country into something worthwhile. We need something more imaginative than Bill C-48 to build a greater Canada with greater opportunity.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE LOANS TO $75,000 FOR IMPROVEMENT OF FARMS, BUSINESSES OR FISHERIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank you for this opportunity to make a few comments on Bill C-48.
It is a pleasure for me tonight to speak on behalf of the professional fishermen farmers and small businessmen in my riding.
First, when after a hard winter the first signs of spring appear in my area, all waterside residents make marvellous dreams about fishing.
They all want to throw their nets and come to their friends with a miraculous catch story. Unfortunately, many if not all have been sorely disappointed lately. Let us imagine, Mr. Speaker, that until now, as I said earlier, when the southern wind brings the ice away, those people would throw their nets, either to catch some herrings, to have some surplus of fish for canning and salting in summer, or to catch cod, what we call "boette"; but now, without even being heard, they have been denied the right to throw their nets. You can imagine, Mr. Speaker, the disappointment of all those people.
Tonight, I would simply like to say a few words to present their case. What is affected is not only herring fishing, but also lobster, clam and various other kinds of fishing in the St. Lawrence and the Chaleur Bay.
As I said a while ago, Mr. Speaker, I should like to speak on behalf of these people, so that they may be allowed to catch a few fish to feed their own families and put some away for future meals. The hon. Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Kaplan) talked a while ago about loans and I am all for them, but I feel that the amount of these loans is quite inadequate. People used to say: if the Social Credit

May 2, 1977
Improvement Loans
Party of Canada ever comes to power, there will be inflation, unemployment, this and that. Although we are not yet in power, inflation is already with us.
In all circumstances of our lives, we are suffering because of inflation. In fact, $75,000 is not very much when one considers the current costs of fishing tackles, for they can hardly pay for the rigging and chain to secure a trawling anchor. This is the type of trawler which the people from the Gaspe and Magdalen Islands areas build especially to go fishing, a fine little boat indeed with a speed of between 10 to 12 nautical miles an hour, and in my opinion, $75,000 is hardly enough to buy the rigging to anchor it securely.
As far as the interest rate is concerned, I wonder what we have in mind to want to charge a penalty to help our brothers, to help someone, to help our people here to expand and develop. This country can give loans without interest for periods of up to 50 years to unknown people, who are probably kind, and who want to bloom and prosper. But then we say we want to help our people, and we punish them, we penalize them. Hence we, of the Social Credit Party, say this: If we really want to help our small industry, our fishermen, our farmers to expand and grow, we should give them loans which are interest free, not loans of $75,000 but loans of up to $300,000 and even more, for a period of 15 years, at administration cost. This would have the effect of really helping those people, and the government could prove to the Canadian people that it really wants its people, its industry, its workers to be proud of belonging to this beautiful and great country which is called Canada.
To my mind, Mr. Speaker, that is the only solution if we really want to put back some order where there has been disorder, and see to it that capital is put at the disposal of all those men and women who are intent on developing the country, on bringing its wealth to fruition, on bringing up families and making of our country one where life is good, where people do not have to worry about the future and where people will be proud to say: We are Canadians, regardless of where we come from, whether it be from the Pacific or the Atlantic, regardless of the tongue we speak or religion we follow, but fully and equally Canadians.
There is much talk of minorities. I find it somewhat childish because the word "minority" should not exist in a country such as ours. We are all equal. We are all entitled to the same things. Why then speak of minorities and thus discriminate?
Mr. Speaker, I would like the few remarks I have just made on Bill C-48 to be taken seriously into consideration. I would like the government, which claims to be democratic, to have some consideration for the small and average business, for our farmers and fishermen. You know, life is no sinecure for the fishermen and farmers who toil from morn till night during the summer months, at the mercy of the whims of the weather, catches and crops. I believe everyone will agree that what I have said is reasonable, and that all those businesses should be granted interest-free loans, at cost, to prove, as I said before, that life is good in that country called Canada.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE LOANS TO $75,000 FOR IMPROVEMENT OF FARMS, BUSINESSES OR FISHERIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to enter this debate, even though belatedly.
May I take this belated opportunity to congratulate the new Minister of State for Small Business (Mr. Marchand) on his appointment to his portfolio. I am glad to note that he is taking his time in trying to obtain input from a substantial proportion of the country's businessmen. Let me explain that I have followed his activities with great concern, even to the point of reading carefully the speech he delivered to the Vancouver Board of Trade on March 21, 1977. I shall quote part of that speech because I think it contains some good ideas. I hope that with the co-operation of the other members of the cabinet he will be able to put them into effect. The minister said:
I have often heard, for example, that small business can't get close to government. It can't find out what programs exist to benefit the small operator, because there are too few channels of communication.
I agree with him wholeheartedly. I continue quoting:
To improve communication between the small business community and the federal government, therefore, I am asking the Federal Business Development Bank to assume the role of being the one-stop contact point.
I will quarrel with that point later in my address. I continue quoting:
The small businessman or woman who needs help or assistance, but doesn't know the way to penetrate the maze of government departments-
I could not agree with him more.
-can pick up the phone and call the FBDB and get the information from one source.
I quarrel with that point.
The FBDB will embark on a publicity and communications program to get the message out to small business that they are available to help.
In terms of access to government assistance, I have been hearing from a number of small processors and manufacturers who would like to benefit from the kinds of innovation assistance like PEP and PAIT and IDAP and similar 'alphabet soup' programs.
I agree with him again.
But they say the terms of reference are too strict, and the turn-around time while Ottawa makes a decision too long to be of benefit to a small company with a short time horizon on a planned project.
So, on April 1st, I am happy to announce, the enterprise development program will absorb these innovations and the adjustment assistance programs into one operation with regional decision-making and terms of reference more favourable to the small operator.
The focus of assistance under this new program structure will be on those promising small and medium sized firms in the manufacturing and processing sectors, that are prepared to undertake projects which are of relatively high risk for their resources, but which could bring attractive rates of return on the total investment.
The small business community has told me that government must support entrepreneurs willing to take a risk on a good idea. I have therefore ensured that the risk factor will count more in the EDP decision-making process, so that small firms will have a better chance of benefiting from federal assistance.
Many of my colleagues have expressed their support for Bill C-48, the bill which would amend the Farm improvement Loans Act, the Small Businesses Loans Act, and the Fisheries
May 2, 1977

Improvement Loans Act, and 1 do so also. In light of what the minister said, I wish to point out that there are still some deficiencies in the three acts. Rather than help the small businessman, they confuse him because of the jungle of bureaucracy which exists between the application and the approval, and because of some of the glaring weaknesses in the legislation which defeat its supposed purpose.
The minister can increase the amount of a loan from $50,000 to $75,000, $500,000 or $1 million. However, many potential small businessmen will never be able to take advantage of a loan because the various agencies through which the loans are directed do not fulfil their roles. All they provide is lip service assistance.
I have been following the progress of these three programs intently. The first thing I wonder about is why there is a need for three programs. A small businessman is just as the word implies, whether he is a fisherman, farmer, operates a sawmill, a small processing plant or confectionary store. A fisherman catches fish at a certain cost for gear, fuel, and other incidentals and tries to sell it at a profit. A farmer grows vegetables, raises poultry or beef at a certain cost, and hopes to dispose of whatever he grows or raises at a profit. But instead of having one program we have created a bureaucracy, an involvement with other levels of government under various other agencies, all of which only creates confusion and discouragement.
The first culprit in the jungle is the chartered banks which show a complete lack of responsibility in most cases, mainly because of their greed. In most cases when a small businessman, fisherman or farmer applies for a government guaranteed loan and is a good risk, the bank manager steers him away from the government loan, because he has to give a preferred rate of interest, to a conventional loan for which he can get an extra 3 or 4 per cent.
I have had many examples of this over the years, and was told by the then finance minister to get the instances in writing and to pass them along to the department. However, on each occasion I have been given some ridiculous tale of woe by the guaranteed loans administration supporting the particular bank's refusal. This is not good enough and I hope the minister will look into this matter seriously.
This is borne out by the quarterly figures produced by the Department of Finance. Let me quote some figures at random. Under the Small Businesses Loans Act from January to September, 1975, in my province of Newfoundland, only 11 loans were granted for a total of $186,000. In comparison, in the province of Prince Edward Island 57 loans were approved totalling $637,000. In Nova Scotia 73 loans were approved totalling over $1 million, and in New Brunswick 154 loans amounting to over $2 million.
There must be some significance in the fact that Prince Edward Island, with one fifth the population and presumably a proportionate number of businessmen, would receive five times as many small business loans as the province of Newfoundland. It should be obvious that the chartered banks in New-
Adjournment Debate
foundland should be taken to task for this evident lack of responsibility toward their role in serving Canadians regardless of where they live.
The greatest weakness in the act is, I repeat, the conglomeration of programs existing under the various departments of government. To my mind it is typical of the pyramid building which goes on within the government by the various ministers who, rather than help, create discouragement, confusion, and a lack of faith in government.
Under the various departments of government there are 62 financial assistance programs supposedly directed toward the small and medium sized businessman. In addition there are 37 non-financial assistance programs in existence. That totals 99 programs with separate bureaucratic staff at a time when the government is supposedly cutting down staff and practising restraint in spending.
If that is not ridiculous enough, there are more related provincial programs with federal financial support. In the province of Newfoundland there are another 31 financial assistance programs with another 30 non-financial programs making a total of 160 programs, all supposedly directed to helping the potential small businessman.
What I presume to be even more ridiculous is that if the province of Newfoundland has 61 financial and non-financial assistance programs, there must be a like number in the other nine provinces. According to guestimates, there must be 700 or 800 government programs directed to the potential entrepreneur who is trying to get government assistance to take advantage of his knowledge of the surrounding resources.
Getting back to the role of the chartered banks which have a close responsibility to the three phases of the legislation which we are debating tonight, it is interesting to note the remarks elicited from supposed experts on the matter. J. K. Finlayson, deputy chairman and executive vice-president of the Royal Bank of Canada, told a conference recently that the chartered banks are heavily and aggressively committed to supporting independent business to the amount of $41/2 billion and that independent businessmen are the backbone of his business. What famous words! All I can ask is: where in the name of all that is decent would the chartered banks be if it were not for small business?
As it is approaching the hour of adjournment, Mr. Speaker, may I call it ten o'clock?

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: CONFEDERATION-SUGGESTION PRIME MINISTER MAKE SPEECH IN THE HOUSE ON NATIONAL UNITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my contribution tonight arises out of a response I received from the President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen) with respect to a simple inquiry I made about the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) who is holding himself out as the saviour of our nation. I asked the reason why he has not yet made one speech in the House of Commons with regard to the whole question of national unity.
The problem is that the Prime Minister speaks on no issues in the House of Commons. He is proceeding to downgrade parliament as he has done since becoming Prime Minister of this country. I submit with all sincerity that the Prime Minister is afraid to speak in the House of Commons on this issue. I will point out a number of reasons for this before my seven minutes are over.
The Prime Minister is the pastmaster of speaking in contrived setup, predetermined types of forums such as television. He had a wonderful opportunity to speak before the American Congress. He loves an opportunity to speak when there is no participation by his peers or other people who have involved themselves in being elected to the House of Commons.
The Prime Minister is not prepared to deal with his peers in the House of Commons on the most important issue facing Canada today. He avoids the House of Commons. It is not good enough for the President of the Privy Council to say that the Prime Minister appears for question period and answers questions relating to national unity. We in the House of Commons know that during the course of the question period, because of our rules, it is possible for the Prime Minister, and he does this on every occasion, simply to slough off the answers. He does not answer questions put to him with respect to what he is prepared to do to maintain national unity. He has not come forward with any positive, constructive proposals but avoids the issue and even attempts to exacerbate the differences which exist between different parts of the country.
When the Prime Minister last spoke about this subject he did so before the National Association of Broadcasters in the course of what was said to be a significant address in western Canada. The speech was televised by the CBC which buckled under government pressure-they are very concerned, now, that they are not giving enough time to the government; cabinet ministers are all whining that the CBC does not think of the balance in broadcasting. The CBC is very sensitive now, so when the Prime Minister's office says it is time to make a significant statement they are naturally going to televise that speech in Winnipeg on the subject of national unity. Quite frankly, the speech was a large bore and has been generally acknowledged by any independent observers of what is going on in our country as being exactly that.

speechtext:
The Prime Minister has done more, I think, individually to bring the country into a crisis of breaking up than any Prime Minister in our history.
What was the promise of 1968? It was to bring this country together. And what have we got? We have Rene Levesque. After nine years under Liberal rule we find a separatist government in the province of Quebec. That is the Prime Minister's record. In 1968 something like 11 per cent of the people of Quebec were in support of a separate state for the province. Now the figure has grown to 25 per cent. The hypocrisy of this man in not coming before parliament to present his case and debate it in the House is beyond contempt.
The Prime Minister supported Premier Bourassa, head of the government which was turned out by the Parti Quebecois in the last election. Now he tells us he is the saviour of our country. But he does not have the courage to come before parliament.
He avoids issues of substance in the province of Quebec. He ignores the existence of mass unemployment in that province, a situation which adds fodder to the flames as far as separatism is concerned. He ignores an unemployment rate of 11 per cent and suggests we place our faith in him-a man who refuses to face parliament and who assures us that everything will be all right. He relies exclusively, in speeches outside the House, on support for his insensitive application of the official bilingual program, an insensitivity which the Commissioner of Official Languages, Mr. Keith Spicer, says has destroyed the will of many Canadians to make the program work. Though the program is acknowleged by the Prime Minister himself to be a failure, he refuses to come before parliament to debate the issue.
The arrogance shown toward parliament is also demonstrated toward provincial governments. He has shown he is only interested in a policy of confrontation. I suggest the Prime Minister has a duty to speak before parliament rather than avoid the issue and speak in contrived, set-up, predetermined television appearances across the country. The speech that the Prime Minister delivered in Winnipeg was a very good example. He should have made the speech some days earlier when he was in Disneyland; it would have been more appropriate to the content of the speech.
I see Your Honour is about to rise, and I know that you are nodding in agreement with the point I am making.

speechtext:
If the members who are bellowing across the way need any evidence of that, I refer them specifically to a recent event which took place in the home town of the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar, the city of Saskatoon, where the Prime Minister was welcomed enthusiastically by a crowd of 5,000 people who demonstrated their dedication to Canadian unity in no uncertain terms, and provided clear evidence of their confidence in the ability of this Prime Minister to deal with this crucial issue in the most effective fashion.
While the issues affecting our national unity in Canada today have not been the direct subject of a major debate in this Chamber recently, they have been the subject of frequent exchanges during other proceedings in this House, and the Prime Minister is fully available and fully capable of handling all questions and comments which may be directed his way for response.
As for the requirement of a full scale House debate on the subject, the Prime Minister and indeed all the House leaders have indicated, at least informally, that they are prepared and indeed anxious to consider such a proposal and will want to discuss it among themselves. These discussions, I presume, will take place this week so that a proper opportunity at an early date will be available to members of parliament to air their views fully on this important area of concern to all Canadians.
I conclude simply by pointing out that it is of interest to note that in recent days the Conservative party has suddenly discovered an interest in national unity. I venture to suggest that they are rather green with envy at the triumphant national successes of the Prime Minister in Quebec City, Washington, Winnipeg, Saskatoon, Allan, and North Battleford, all successful speeches by the Prime Minister which have articulated very well indeed the case for national unity, and in terms which certainly have not been matched by any hon. gentlemen sitting across the way, particularly the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Hnatyshyn) who spoke this evening.

AIRPORTS-VICTORIA, B.C.-REASON FOR FAILURE TO INSTALL RADAR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that outburst we have just had is not going to be a difficult act to follow.
On March 29 of this year, during one of my interventions in this House in regard to the need for radar at Victoria International Airport, the minister endeavoured to cloud the issue in his usual manner by a diversionary stratagem which is used all too frequently by the government. He started to talk about something else. He started to boast about the high level of safety which we have at Canadian airports. I do not question these high standards of safety; I welcome them. But I want to improve them; hence my suggestion, Mr. Speaker.
I do wonder about the growing use of an airport where all safety devices are not available. I say growing because from 1972 to 1976 traffic at this airport increased from 115,000 flights in and out to 186,000 flights in and out. These are flights of all sorts of aircraft where binoculars are still used to detect the presence of other aircraft. Binoculars are used also to determine altitude, speed, and course of aircraft in the area. This is reminiscent of the training I got 35 to 36 years ago in aircraft recognition so that I could recognize a JU-88 before he recognized me. You will remember that, Mr. Speaker. This training was in aircraft recognition so that I could tell a Stuka from a Lysander, so that I would know which to shoot down and which to allow to fly off. Using binoculars for safety purposes dates from those days.
The Minister may think I am arguing for terminal radar- IFR control sets. Not at all. What I am pleading for is surveillance radar, which is something more sophisticated than binoculars to help the controllers in cloudy weather and at night to know what is in the air, where it is, how high it is, what direction it is going, and at what speed, so that the controllers in turn can use this information during the landings and take-offs of other aircraft that are in the air and in the proximity and using that airport, be they commercial or private. That is all-surveillance radar.
We had a fatal accident at Victoria International Airport just about a year ago. That is what brought this whole exercise on. An aircraft, which was not familiar with the area, was above cloud and was being directed from the ground and was being informed on how to find the airport from the ground. Had there been radar at that airport, the controllers would have known where exactly it was. According to its last reported position from the aircraft as to position, course and speed, it might have been at A or at B. Directions given to it on the assumption it was at A would have meant a safe landing. Those instructions given to it when it was actually at B brought disaster. That is why we need surveillance radar.
The minister tried to take some snide shots at me the other day during one of my questions about Victoria boasting of beautiful weather. No one in his senses would say we never have rain in Victoria. Otherwise, how would we grow our fruits

and flowers? Rain means clouds. It is as simple as that. Binoculars do not penetrate clouds. I will spell it out if the minister cannot understand it. Radar does. The minister argues his staff feels we do not need radar because our traffic mix is not the one that calls for radar.
Mirabel worked up to 49,000 flights in total in 1976, of which 42,000 were commercial flights. They worked up to 49,000 flights, and they have got pretty sophisticated radar. Victoria had 184,000 flights the same year, and 49,000 of them were commercial. Victoria had 16 per cent more commercial flights than Mirabel. These large commercial aircraft nearly all have their own radar screens which can detect nearby aircraft.
We had more than 100,000 flights in and out last year. They consisted of local flights of small aircraft relying on VFR and what they can learn from the air traffic controllers. These aircraft flew in cloudy conditions and at night. This mix of aircraft, commercial and heavy aircraft, does call for surveillance radar. It would provide eyes to our air traffic controllers. I am just as interested in safety as is the minister. I appeal once again to the minister to take this matter seriously and to go back to his staff and have them examine the situation and provide surveillance radar at Victoria International Airport.

speakeroldname: Mr. Marcel Roy (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: AIRPORTS-VICTORIA, B.C.-REASON FOR FAILURE TO INSTALL RADAR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to begin this debate by first assuring the hon. member that the unavailability of radar at the Victoria International Airport by no means undermines flight safety. The air traffic control procedures in use are designed to give maximum assurance that the control tower at Victoria is aware of the position of all aircraft about to enter or operate within their area of control.
The decision to install radar is based on a number of factors, including traffic mix, weather conditions, land characteristics and, of course, the movements of aircraft, proceeding to and from an airport under instrument flight rules. Further, as the minister has mentioned in the House, the installation of a radar system is done on a priority need basis and taking into account the finances which are available for this purpose.
As the hon. member is aware, the question of the installation of radar at the Victoria International Airport has been a matter of study for some time now by officials in the Department of Transport. There remain significant study and analyses to be carried out before a final solution, which would likely involve both short and long term recommendations, can be suggested. So it will be some time before decisions will be taken on the situation.
In the meantime, as part of the short term plans, improved air traffic control procedures taking into account unique traffic patterns at Victoria are being examined. In March, 1977, air traffic controllers from the Pacific region carried out a week long study at the ATS simulation centre in Hull with a goal to examining procedures for the Vancouver-Victoria area.

In closing, Mr. Speaker, I would like to reiterate the minister's stand that Canada has maintained an extremely high standard of air safety of which Canada can be very proud.

CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION-BEDFORD, N.S.-DIVERSION OF LAND FROM HOUSING PURPOSES TO USE AS MUNICIPAL DUMP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the issue that brings us together this evening would, at first blush, seem to be a municipal issue, but there are two federal departments or agencies involved. A number of years ago the city of Halifax, the city of Dartmouth and the county of Halifax on behalf of the suburbs of the two cities mentioned, began a search for a new dump, and being properly inclined toward language of the twentieth century, they decided to call it a landfill site. What they are looking for is a joint municipal dump.
Studies were carried out and the first place that was found advantageous for such a landfill site or dump was a portion of the city of Dartmouth. But the council there, in its wisdom, said this was an area that could be used for industrial land, and since we all bow and scrape before the bitch goddess of commerce, it was decided that there should be no dump in the city of Dartmouth.
The second suggestion was that it be located on a side road in the growing county area of Sackville. Some protests were made about this on the grounds that it imposed an environmental hazard and also was too close to residential areas. These arguments had their effect, so the group, a regional group backed by the province of Nova Scotia, went elsewhere.
The third area was in the black community. That would not do because they might be charged with discrimination. So they went to a fourth area, Jack Lake, which served primarily a white community. In any event, it was serviced by a main highway which, on balance, is a good idea since the heavy trucks which carry the garbage should travel on main highways and not skitter down side streets through heavily populated school sections. That is the advantage of Jack's Lake, but the major disadvantage is that it is too close to both the unincorporated area of Sackville, which soon will be the third largest municipal area of Nova Scotia when it is incorporated, and to the area of Bedford.
In Bedford there were fights over the years, so they sensibly put themselves together into what is called the Bedford Service Commission, and they are prepared to tackle anybody. They certainly tackled the people involved in trying to put the dump near their community. I notice the parliamentary secretary shares with me the old school tie; he knows the story very well, but I have to place it on the record.
Earlier today I asked the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) if it was true that there was some attempt to go ahead with a lease of the Jack's Lake facility, owned by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, for the dump. He said that the opinion of the Department of Justice was being sought. I might add that the government depart-

ment involved is the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, which could be making grants toward the establishment of this landfill site or dump. In any event, the minister indicated that an approach was being made to the Department of Justice.
I have two objections which I will state. The Bedford Service Commission is a scrappy group of people which is prepared to raise the money and put it where its mouth is. It fought this issue all the way. It won in the lower court. It lost in the appeal court in Nova Scotia. It then went to the Supreme Court of Canada in its battle with the Attorney General of Nova Scotia and the Halifax-Dartmouth Regional authority. It obtained from Chief Justice Bora Laskin and Justices Martland, Judson, Ritchie, Spence, Pigeon, Dickson, Beetz and de Granpre judgment on three grounds: first, that the appellants, the Attorney General of Nova Scotia and the Halifax-Dartmouth Regional Authority, left somebody out, namely, Mrs. Lacona Heather Cunningham, in their initial appeal to the appeal court of Nova Scotia; second, and I quote from the opinion:
... the allegations in the statement of claim, taking them as established (as we must for the purpose of the present proceedings) do raise justiciable issues, and we are further of the opinion that the appellant Bedford Service Commission ... has a sufficient interest to challenge the legality of the proposed establishment of a sanitary landfill, by or under the authority or with the approval of the respondents, on a site within the area in which the appellant is empowered to act under its powers and in respect of its functions, and, hence, to assert the claims that it has advanced in the statement of claim.
My point, therefore, is twofold. First the Supreme Court of Canada decision is saying that there should be full speed ahead for the Bedford Service Commission to fight what it regards to be right in the lower court, and I think that they are absolutely right in that. We cannot allow people to be miffed or mad about something unless they have a chance to go somewhere and assert their claims. Second, the minister and the parliamentary secretary have been very co-operative with me, but a member of the minister's office indicated to me that they would wait until a court decision came in. I find it passing strange.
I do not know from whence the pressure is coming. I do not know whether it is coming from the provincial government in Nova Scotia or these three municipalities. Now they are prepared to go to justice, to ask for an opinion as to whether CMHC can enter into a lease whereby this land can be used as a landfill site. I think that if they were to do that, or if the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) or people in his department were to allow it, or counsel it to be done, or if the people working at CMHC permitted this to be done, or if I were to remain silent on the issue, I think we would all be in contempt of the Supreme Court of Canada.
It has been said that the Bedford Service Commission has the right to take its fight somewhere. Surely to God they should be allowed to have that fight. If it goes against the

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Robert Gauthier (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State for Urban Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subtopic: CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION-BEDFORD, N.S.-DIVERSION OF LAND FROM HOUSING PURPOSES TO USE AS MUNICIPAL DUMP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have had occasion to discuss this subject with the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants (Mr. McCleave) and, on some occasions, to look further into the matter by meeting with representatives of the Bedford Service Commission and other interested groups in the Halifax area. I visited the area on February 4 and heard what interested parties had to say about the landfill site at Jack's Lake. The hon. member referred to it as a dump. I suggest the area has been described in other terms. For instance, it has been referred to as a solid waste disposal area, or as a sanitary landfill area. Perhaps such terms are more appropriate. I do not think that the area in question is a dump.
The federal government, through CMHC, must act within the zoning and planning legislation and processes of the province and the municipality. CMHC has no authority to establish or revise permitted land use within a municipality. The responsibility for this rests properly at the provincial-municipal level.
However, CMHC has a responsibility to ensure that any land use is not incompatible with environmental requirements. As a point of interest, the proposed temporary use of this parcel of land at Jack's Lake coming under the partnership arrangement involving Nova Scotia and CMHC, has been examined jointly by the federal and provincial departments of the environment and CMHC. Standards for the development, operations, and final restoration of the site have been established by this joint authority.
The minister's decision on the signing of the lease will not depend upon the outcome of the court case to which the hon. member referred. His decision, as he has previously stated, will depend upon the opinion of the Department of Justice as to the legal authority of CMHC to enter into such a lease. I am told that this opinion will be handed down shortly.
I said at the beginning of my comments that I am well aware of this problem and sympathize with the Bedford Service Commission group. I have great respect for the knowledge, logic, and rationale they have displayed and understand their concerns. The minister is also well aware of the many aspects of this controversial case, if I may use that word, and we, as responsible people, are waiting for a legal opinion from the Department of Justice. We expect to obtain it in the near future, after which the minister will be in a position to take a decision in accordance with and based on his responsibilities.
